LADIES • LETTER.
MT DEAR NMLIE,

Till the welcome approach of summer tells us to put velvet and dark shades aside—unless one is rabid to be in the very latest cry, we must be contest with the following pretty toque. The shape is of fine black felt; the brim bee a double bind (or fold) and lining of purple velvet. The crown is showered over the lett side and the left side tilts up. A black feather stands up from the upturned brim. A novelty in neck rear consists of a very thick ruche ot purple mousseline inter- spersed with big bunches of violets; twp very full stole ends coming therefrom in the front being caught at intervals by bunches of the saute. This is a very pretty and becoming boa for a Milder days, when fur is not necessary, and would g 9 admirably with the toque described. A linen collar would look well should the weather become warmer.

The ssle season is a particularly happy periGd for the practical meter of many small folks, for whom the "short lengths" (which always prove too short to be of any real use for grown ups) are more often than not most useful; and some quite dazzling results often follow the purchase of some of these same lengths, both for smarter wear and knockabou., school wherewithal. Kilted skirts make very pretty wear for children, and are so easy to make. The fashions for young folks nowadays are exceedingly pretty', and a certain simplicity of style characterises them all, a fact to be specially noted. Berge frocks in navy blue or crimson are always becoming and warm, and suitable for, school, and no one can go wrong in aeleoting one of these for everyday wear. •

A coat faced with rather wide chinchilla revers and showing a white silk and lace front with a knot or two of bright, soft, rose-coloured panne, is about as becoming a garment as may be imagined. In fact the arrangement is in itself so very pretty that one feels rattier disappointed if the face above it is not pretty too! Blondes, who dare not wear rose colour in daylight, may substitute sky blue or pale, bright sapphire blue, a lovely, and nob sufficiently appreciated colour. A sash of crepe- de.chine may be passed round the waist, fastening at the left side under a rosette of this crepe, with long ends falling to the hem of the skirt. The hat used may be of black velvet, piped under the brim with white satin, or any colour matching the sash. A large rosette in c,loured panne, with two black feathers, might complete the trimming.

All of the mourning gowns I have noticed lately -are once more extensively trimmed with crape, but in the case of widows' mourning it is no longer lonsidered necessary to have the dress completely overed with the costly and unserviceable material; n fact, there is often but little difference between the gown worn during the first year of widowhood and that adopted by a daughter in mourning for a parent. Crape-cloth, parramatta, and cashmere are still the three favourite materials for mourning costumes, and the crape trimming is generally pplied in the form of tucks. One stylish deep qourning dress is of fine crape-cloth, and has the 'ightly-trained clinging skirt bordered with three raduated crape tucks, while the bodice, pouched little in front, has revers of crape and a pointed oat of the same arranged in close tucks, which are leo used to trim the tops of the tight sleeves. nother model has a deep plain filsunce of crape •ound the skirt, over which the parrarnatta top is ..rranged to simulate a pointed tunic edged with three very narrow folds of crape. The bodice is out pinafore fashion, the top bordered with folds of ..rape, and the yoke composed entirely of finely- ucked crape. For slighter mourning, dull-surfaced loth is a fashionable material, and for trimmings mourning silk, dull jet, and black silk gauze are largely used. The peplum has caught on so well during the last iew months that many of the handsomest dinner gowns are made with overskirts fashioned in this way. In jet or beads these long pointed polonaises, as they may almost be called, are unavoidably heavy. Later on, they will probably be seen in cloth or cashmere, slightly differing in tone, or wholly in material, from the skirt beneath. A red velvet peplum over a darker red silk skirt would be an effective dinner gown, with the bodice ouA up in smaller points to carry out the idea of the large ones on the skirts. There is sometimes a central point, and one at either side, with a very long one at the back; but occasionally two suffice for the front. A ball dress, prepared for one of the numerous dances projected at the beginning of this season, but postponed till happier times, was in white lace with peplum of pearl, and crystal, and opalescent heads. It was a lovely gown.
Your loving,
JaNiqm THE MOST NUTRITIOUS.

div.p: MABEL FLORENCE WATKINS.

That persistent, !seeking cough bangs on becAuse the system is weak. The reason most specifics only afford temporary relief is because they do not enable the system to overcome its own weakne4s. and thus have the resistive power to ward off a return of the trouble.

The quicker people begin to think about the real standard of their healte, and thus look beneath their shronic ailments, the sooner will they begin the treatment of their chronic ailments from an intelli- gent stAndpoint. You can prove the truth of this assertion by consulting any medical man in this or any other enlightened country. ludeed, the whole praetiee of medicine is the helping of Nature to help herself.

The litt!e girl whose photograph we herewith re- produce, was unquestionably in a lew state of vital- ity, or she would not have had a bad cough all through one winter. The following letter tells about tho treatment of her case : "kielhorne, Minerva Avenue. "I)arten Road, Dever, Kent, "15th My, 1899. _

"Dear Sirs,—lt gives me great' pleasure to be able to testify to the value of Scott's Emulsion. My wko had just turned three and a half years, had hPen suff,lring from a very bad cough all last winter. We tried everything we could think of, but all to no use. She was gettisg so very weak and thin, we bevan to he very much troubled

alydit her. We thought we would try Scstt's Emulsion, and after the first bottle or so we (mild see she wee improving. She made such headway that she lost the cough she had, and began to get quite strong again. Then she had a very bad attack of tonsilitie, which made her very bad again, but we persevered with the Emulsion, and I firmly beieve had we not done so, it woutd have gone hard with her. Thanks to Scott's Emulsion, however, she is well and strong again ; in fact, she looks the picture ef health.
" I maim. yours truly, (Signed)." F.. S. WATIINg." - ,

, Thus you see the power of Scott's Emulsion to overc,me the weak tandenees et the system. It is a specific for coughs and colds, and in fact all throat and lung affections, because it contains cod-liver oil and glycerine, bcth of which are standard remedial agents. But Scott's Emulsion is much more than a specific, becaose it presents the oil in a form that is easily digested and quickly absorbed. Consequently when the oil is once in the blood, it quickly re- stores vitality to the system, and in this way raises the standard of health. Seott's Emulsion is per- fectly palatable, and easy for anybody to take. You can obtain a sample of Scott's Emulsion by sending threepence to cover postage to Scott and Bowne, Limited, Manufacturing Chemists, 95, Great Saffron Hill, London, EC., and mentioning this paper. div.head: "WOMEN'S CHAT."
div.p: "WOMEN'S CHAT."

Our Royal Family have all along shown themselves in sympethy with the spirit of the nation, by availing themselves of every opportunity of displaying their admiration for, and gratitude towards, the soldiers and sailors who are fighting for their country in South Africa. The Prince of Wales bas, on many coca dons, inspected regiments or detachments, about to proceed to the front,the Princess of Wales was mainly instrumental in securing the despatch of the hospital ship which bears her name, and the Duke of Connaught has fre- quently shown his interest in the troops,whetber Volun- teers, or members of the regular army, by attending to see them off. Both the Duchess of Connaught and Princess Henry of Battenberg have been present at func- tions of this description, and yet other members of our Royal Mouse have testified in one way or anether their eerdial feeling towards our brave men. We have often beard, or read about the spectacle of a "nation in arms" but the picture was probably never better represented than it is just now in South Africa by the people of the Dutch Republics. If anythirg, the women appear to 13'3 more embittered against the British than the men, and many are actively assisting the Boers in comrnisrariat or other duties at the front. General Joubert is always and everywhere accompanied by his wife, who personally provides for her husband's requirements. On one occasion in the early stages of the war, the General was seen directing operations,and at the sa-ne time munching a mutton chop, which he held unceremoniously in his hand, and which his wife had just cooked. The present war is, of course, no new experience of fighting for Mrs. Joubert, and many of the older Boer women, though it is naturally somewhat different to the old times, and the native campaigns, when the women in the !eager handed up the guns, and melted bullets for their husbands. When Mrs. Joubert was shown, some years ago, an interesting collection of ancient pewter in Amsterdam, she remarked how useful it would he, to make bullets of !" Not only have the authorities hitherto approached the Volunteer movements with the large,t possible amount of red tape, but in many instances, the medical depart- ment appears to have raised needless objections,aed some amusing stories are told about the rejection of volunteers anxious to go out to the war. One man who was otherwise quite fit, was put back on account of bad teeth, when he protested that they had been good enough for him for many years past, and all he wanted was to go out and fight the Boers and not Irn eat them ! several others have been rejected who afterwards had no difficulty in insuring their lives as perfectly sound. There is no better way to ascertain whether there are any grounds for alerm about the state of one's health than to go to a Life Insurance Office with a proposal. Many vonenteere offered their services in ignorance of the f .ct that only unmarried men were accepted,and not a few, no doubt, saw in African adventure, an opportu- nity to leave domestic trials and worries to others. One man on being told that he was disqualified because be was married, expressed surprise, and asked the sergeant if he supposed that" he'd want to go if he was'nt ?" Khaki is a colour en evidence everywhere, and it is scmething to be thankful for that there is no better or more useful one, for hard, and everyday wear. The idea is of course intended as a compiiment to our gallant troops in Seuth Africa, and it is astonishing bow impor- tant a personage the soldier has become since the war broke out. Nothing could be more suitable than the new Khaki serge for cycling, and it will probably be in great demand later on, for country and seaside wear. Why. I wonder, do fah ion plates represent women with such extraordinary figures ? As a matter of fact we generally walk more perpendicularly than men, but it there were a woman the shape of a fashion plate, and two straight poles placed one behind acd one in front of her we should get this remarkable result. The one placed next to the bust would touch the ground about eighteen inches in advance of her toes, and that placed against her back hair, would touch the ground twenty- four inches nem her neck. Allowing ten inches for 'the length of the boot, and nothing for the hat, the woman would require in a creved a 'pace of fifty-two inches by sixteen or eighteen, which, as Euclid would have said " is absurd."

These pictures remind me of a story which is told by Sir John Adye. The War Office issued instructions that if a recruit was of minimum height, his chest measure- ment was to be so many inches, and if he exceeded that height, the chest measurement was to cenforia to a certain scale. Some weeks later an old recruiting aergeant was called to accourat by an officer because he had not brought in any recruits. "Beg parden, air," he replied, "but nature never yet made a man the shape you want 'em sir !" Dainty little sprin capes are in course of construction at all leading modist s. Some are single. some double with cods reaching to the waist. The majority are being built of cloth, embroidered in chenille and lined with Bilk. It is clnubtf 01 though if these particular garments will gain any great hold upon our affections. The light, Uttle r,,,,tt is a ;Tore. becoming and dasirab!ecover- ing, from many points of view and we shall probably

cling to it in preference to anything ofered us in the cane variety. It may be doubted whether domestic servants, who bslong to the Salvation Army, are better in any particu- lar respect than other classes. The experience of many is indeed quite to the contrary though this may be said without any disparagement to the great and noble work which the Army carries on in the course of humanity. It seems, however, that many domestic servants who belong to the Army, have become troubled in their minds respecting some of the ordinary Customs of society, and they have suggested that it is a "wbite lie" to say " not at home "to callers, when the mistress is simply not receiving visitors. The subject has conse- quently been considered at headquarters, and in an authoritative statement in the " War Cry " it is announced that there need be no objection to the custom because the expression is not used in the literal sense, but in one that is universally understood by society. So long as there is no intention to deceive,the Army sees no ohjPction to its members conforming to the usual practice. The Government inquiry into the subject of food adulteration continues to elicit startling revelations. We have berAcic acid and other deleterious preservatives in our milk, butter, and many other articles of daily con- sumption, and now it seems that beer, and the lighter wines, are often treated in the same way. According to Professor Corfield, Consulting Sanitary Adviser to the Office e Works, and Medical Officer of Health, Bailey- licaced is used for the purpose. The extreme irritation caused by tills substance may be guessed from the fact that it is used externally for the removal of corns and warts. Mr. Chamberlain recently referred to the neces- sity for establishing a school for brewing, and every now and then we hear something of the so-called Pure Beer movement. It is surely time some progress was made in these directions when one may employ the din- ner beer for the double-barrelled ourposs of refreshment, and the removal of corns and warts. Little do we know all we eat and drink, and in spite of legislation and the increased activity of Government inspectors, weseem to knew less and less in these days when chemical com- pounds and mixtures so frequently take the place of the natural and genuine article. div.head: NOBLER THAN REVENGE.
div.p: NOBLER THAN REVENGE.
BY ESME STUART, Author of "In the Dark," "Inscrutable," "A Woman of Forty," "Sara's Mother," &c.

div.head: CHAPTER XXVI:
div.p: CHAPTER XXVI:

If Ruby could have known that her father ww4 not very angry with her and that Alec was not unhappy at her silence, she would not have been at all miserable in her new life. Mrs. Vernon had taken a great fancy to her, add instead of treating her as an ordinary companion she wished to makn a daughter of her. It was, indeed, difficult to help loving the girl, who was so gentle and so anxious to repay any kindness shewn to her. Dr. Murray often came to see her, and he always led the conversa- tion round to her father. Ruby was only too glad to talk of him, and, strangely enough, Dr. Murray seemed to be very well informed about him, though be did not tell her that Sir Harry was in London, nor that Bob had accompanied him and that James Felton was still with her father.

Ruby did not like to ask too many questions, for the doctor was rather reticent about particulars. It would, perhaps, have been better had he told Ruby that her father was in London; but events occur that are so unexpected that it is impossible to foresee them or to guard against them. Some ten days after the events related in the last chapter Mrs. Vernon asked Dr. Murray to come and have a little talk with her.

"I want to know," said the old lady, giving a searching look at the doctor's face, "all that you can tell me about Ruby. This father of hers does not seem to be much concerned about her, so I think that I shall adopt her. Tell me your opinion." "I cannot tell you more than she has told you. Her father is looking for her, but he has, at present, no clue to her whereabouts."
"And if he finds her will he marry her to a rascal ? "
"I do not doubt it." "Then you think that I need not consider him at all."
The doctor paused a moment. "I cannot tell you for a certainty, but I think that a father who tries to force a husband upon his child deserves no consideration."
"But if I adopt her will be come and claim her ?" "I think that you might refuse to let him have her."

"Humph! Well, I am very fond of the child. She-suits me exactly, and she is the first I havee met who expects nothing of me and who under4' stands Pompey's feelings. "I am sure that she is as good as she looks. What surprises me is that a girl brought up by such an unscrupulous man can be so charming." "The girl is quite natural, but she is very badly educated, and I am trying to remedy this defect. She is well disposed." The doctor smiled. "I think it is a little late to expect much result ; but Ruby is anxious to learn, and she tells me that you are so very kind to her."

"Lluniph!"•said Mrs. Vernon. "I don't think I am. But I like the girl, and if I adopt her I shall leave her all my money. What will her father say to that?" "I hope that he will never know it," said the doctor, again looking amused. "But I must say no more at present.' "You are very mysterious." "I am so much afraid that these rascals will find Ruby before I can unmask them. I want to find Ruby's cousin, Alec Beauworth. It is strange that her father and I and the villain are all look- ing for him, and that at present we cannot dis- cover him. I think that he has been warned, and that he is afraid of their finding him." "Why should he mind?" _ _

"I believe if we knew that we should be nearer a solution of our difficulties. In any case this poor girl saved herself from an awful fate by running away." "You always were a knight-errant, Arthur." "I will get to the bottom of this. I owe it to myself—and to others." 'ln any case, Ruby is certainly very fond of this cruel father," said Mrs. Vernon. • It was a few days later after this conversation that Ruby was sitting reading to Mrs. Vernon. Her face was sad, for she was always thinking of Alec and her father. Oh, when would it be safe to write to Yewdale and to tell her father that it was not because she did not love him that she had fled? But she had promised Dr. Murray not to do anything till he gave her. leave. So she brooded on all the past history of her troubles and longed to tell Alec how she was safe and to ask him why he had gone away without telling her. She could not understand all that had happened, but she longed to see him and to tell him that she had done what he had told her. It must be owned that Ruby did not much attend to her reading this morning. She felt so restless, and so anxious to know what she ought to do. All at once she turned to see why Mrs. Vernon made none of her usual remarks, when, to het horror, she saw that her kind friend was lying with her eyes closed, and that her face was as pale as death. Ruby sprang up and rang the bell. In a moment Mrs. Vernon's old maid, Harris, appeared. "Good gracious, Miss Halkett, mistress has one of her bad faints. Please open that draiver and get me a little bottle you will see there." Ruby did as she was bid, but the drops did not restore Mrs. Vernon. -

"Will you put on your hat and go to the oppo- site side of the square, Miss Halkett, and ask for Dr. Jessop ? He's the nearest, and will you tell Jamei to go for Mrs. Vernon's own doctor or to Dr. Murray? He told me if this ever happened that I was to get a doctor at once—the nearest one." "I will go at once," said Ruby. "And please, miss, be as quick as ever you can to come back. She must be held up and her fore- head bathed." _ _ '
"I will run as fast as I can, Harris." "It's number ninety-nine, you can't mistake it: the name is on the door." _

_ Ruby flew to get her hat and ran downstairs, delivered her message to the footman, and then she rushed out down the street and across the square. She rang the bell, and asked if the dr, tor was at home. _

"so, miss, not at home." Is there another doctor quite close? It is fox a. lady who is very ill." "Yes, miss, if you go to the corner there is another doctor there—Dr. Knight. I am sure he will come."

Ruby ran on. Happily Dr. Knight was at home, and he sent word that he would come immediately. As she turned away Ruby noticed that there was a little side street that would be a shorter way, and without pausing she turned into it instead of return- ing the way she had come. She had not gone three steps when suddenly she found herself face t,o face with James Felton! "The dickens!" he exclaimed.

Both were so much surprised, and Ruby was so much frightened that for half an instant neither of them moved, then Ruby, making a great effort, tried to run past him, but not before he had managed to stretch out his hand and to clutch her arm. Ruby uttered a little scream.

"Let me go! Let me go!" she called out. "Not so fast, young lady, I shan't be taken in twice. Now I've caught you you won't get away again in a hurry, by Gad you shan't!" The street was a lonely one, and with few dwellings in it except mews belonging to the richer houses. At Ruby's scream several grooms came out to see what was taking place. They beheld only a young man dressed in good clothes, and a pretty young lady trying to run away from him. "You must come, Ruby; it's no use your struggling." "I won't come with you." "What's the row?" said a groom, taking a pipe out of his pocket. "She's my wife, and she's trying to run away from me." " I'm not his wife! It's a lie! He is a bad man!"
"They always say that," laughed another man. "No use to interfere between 'usbands and wives." "It's not true! Let me go, James Felton!" "She knows his name, anyhow," laughed the first man. _ _ _
"Oh! please fetch a policeman! I live quite close by here. He can come with me and see if it's 'true."

But the appeal was in vain. James uttered a piercing whistle which, as if by magic, brought a hansom to his side. He almost lifted Ruby into it and gave an address, adding: "Go as quick as possible." Suddenly Ruby realised that it was of no use struggling, the crowd had not believed her. What was she to do? James held her firmly by the wrist, and there was nothing to do but to keep very still and to try and form some elan of escape.
Ifer heart beat so fast that she could hardly realise what she was doing, and she trembled in every limb, but she would not give in. What did It mean?
"Are you taking me to my father?" she said at last, when she could find breath to speak with. "You must! I will se?, him!"

"I'm not quite such a fool," said James Felton. "This time you shall go where I.choose. That precious father of yours let you slip before, and it shan't happen again. No, thank you. Look here, Ruby, can t you be sensible? It will be better for you in the end. I never thought my luck would turn again, but it has." "You are very wicked and I shall never raLrry you. I have been helped and I shall be again. Clod will not let you have your way. Take me to papa, and I will tell him everything." James laughed wildly as he tightened his hold on her.

"You are coming tp my lodgings, and after that you will think better of it." Ruby's eyes flashed indignantly. She looked out of the window which James had closed, and longed to ask some of the passers-by to help her. What could she do? What could she hope for? At last the cab stopped at the door of a small house down a side street off the Strand. James jumped out, but placed himself before the door whilst he paid the driver. Ruby looked to see if it were possible to escape, but James was on his guard; he was not going to be baulked a second time.

• "Now," he said, almost lifting her down from the cab and holding her tightly whilst he walked up the steps, "look here, Ruby, the more noise you make the worse it will be for you." He opened the door with a latch-key, then he half pushed her upstairs, never letting her go for a moment. At the head of the stairs he paused, took a look up and down to make sure that no one had seen him, then he opened his door. Ruby trembled from head to foot as he led her into a small room.

"Sit down," he said. "I daresay now you x.re tired." "I will not sit down. You have no business to bring me here, I have friends, and they will look for me, and you will be punished." As she said this poor Ruby remembered that Mrs. Vernon would be too ill to know anything, except that Ruby had left her in her hour of need. Dr. Murray too would think that she was an impostor. No one could guess what had happened to her, no one would dream that this misfortune had overtaken her without any fault of her own. "Now, Ruby, listen quietly tome. Do not be childish. You have been the cause of a great deal of trouble and a great deal of expense. I have set all the force to find you, but you were so deuced clever that you outwitted them." Ruby looked at James as if she did not under- stand him. It was the look of despair. "Well, as I was sayina, you had better be sensible. You seem tu pick up friends pretty easily. Tell me, have you been with that cousin of yours, eh? A pretty adventure, I daresay. . but it won't do."

Ruby did not anwer. She clasped bet hands tightly together and turned over all the wild possibilities that she could imagine. But she must be calm, it would never do to let James frighten her too much so that she could not act. She looked as pale as death as she stood there, but she would not answer this man. She had made one appeal to him, and that was all she would do. "Well, if you are mute, it makes things easier. Look here, Ruby, I'm in a precious hurry tc get away to Australta. It's getting warm in this country. In any case, you and I can start this evening for the Continent, and I'll write to you' father afterwards, so I advise you to take it easy and to sit down and eat."
Still Ruby remained motionless, andt she would not sit down nor would she speak. At that moment there was a ring at the dom below. James hastened to the window and looked out.
"It's a friend of mine. I must leave you s minute, Ruby. I'm sorry you won't take a chair, but that's your own look-out." He walked to the door, and slipping out, hi locked it.

Ruby could hardly move, but she made a great effort. In his hurry James had left the window open. It was a bright sunny morning. Was there no help? 0 God, no help now? Where was she? She knew so little of London that she conk not guess the locality. A long way, perhaps, from her kind friends. Oh, what would they think of her and what would be her fate? Married by force to that man, or worse. Ruby knew very little of the world, but she knew enough to realise that James would stop at nothing to get her into his power. She looked out, there was no one in the street but one or two working-men going towards the Thames. Ruby had experienced what it meant to shout to the passers-by. All at once she saw a slim man in a big overcoat coming leisurely towards the house. His eyes were fixed on it. Ruby seemed to feel that there was someone who might help her. She did not tall out, but seizing a pencil she wrote on an envelope which was in her pocket, and on which was her name: "Fetch a policeman and save me. Please help me." She beckoned to him and let the envelope fall. At that moment she heard a footstep, for James was coming back. She flew back to the place where he had left her. Would she be saved? She had not even seen if her envelope had been picked up. Would the young man think it was no busi- ness of his? How could a man come to her where she was? Oh, it was useless, but it was her only chance. She would never go away with James that evening as his wife. Never, but- James entered. He looked a little flurried. "Look here, Ruby, I have had some bad news. I have not much time to waste. I am going to order a cab at once and take you to the station. We will go to Dover by the next train, and it's no use your making a fuss. Do you understand? Now take this cake and eat. No fainting, mind, and make haste."

div.head: •-- – • . • • ' • •• • • • • of! •"• "!..11 • • • • 15104.4i:Zi11.• ' • " • :Z"S.
div.p: CHAPTER XXVII.

Bob had by this time become a very sharp messenger. After his fortnight in London, he was also a much sadder individual, for he had to be at Mr. James's beck and call, and this had brought him into strange company. However, Bob's opinion was not asked, nor were his wishes con- sulted. He was left very little time to follow his own inclinations, and Bob's hopes had received a dreadful shock when he found that Mr. Alec had left his lodgings and that no one knew where he was. He was often sent to the firm of architects to ask after Alec, but they had always given the same answer till this very morning, when he was told that Mr. ,Beauworth had returned to his work and that he would be going out at one o'clock if Bob returned at that time, for Mr. Beauworth was not to be disturbed.

Bob knew that he must return at once to tell Mr. James; there was no help for it. Even if he refused he would soon be found out, and then there would be no more chance of saving his friend. As he walked towards James's lodgings off the Strand, Bob turned over and over in his mind what he could do to warn Alec that he would be followed that evening. Sir Harry was still at the hotel, and would hardly move out of it. He had become morose, and his bursts of temper were frequent. James took the lead, and the squire was entirely under his thumb. Bob could make no sense out of it all except that both the men wanted to find Miss Ruby and Mr. Alec. Bob hoped that they would find neither. In his imagination the two had found each other, and were hiding from the squire, and this simple romance satisfied him entirely. As Bob neared the iodgings he saw his old enemy, the slim man in the great coat, coming towards him. "I'm blessed," thought Bob, "if he don't want to know something else. I've seen him* often since that day, and I believe he lives close to us, and that he has takeit a liking for finding out private information." "How do, my friend," said the man, as Bob was passing him, pretending not to see him. "Not much worse than I was before," said Bob. "Thank you, all the same." "Rather sharper, it seems to me. Look here, want you." "Do you? Can't oblige you this morning." "Can't you. We'll see about that." "You can't see no better than you do at this ere present," said Bob. "Oh, yes, I can. Are you going to call upon your friend, Mr. James Felton,' by name? " "I ain't gOing to call on no friend," said Bob, scornfully. "Let, us say an acquaintance.' "You can say that if you please. "• "Then just oblige me by looking at this paper and telling me if you know the name." Bob was not anxious to look, but he so far obliged the inquisitive stranger as to squint at an env(
:iope. DO you know a young lady of the name of Lubv littlkat ? "

"No, 1 don't." "You never heard of such a one? She has nothing to do with your friend up there? " "I ain't got a friend up there, growled Bob. "Sure? Look again, Ruby Halkett. Is it an assumed name?" "A what?" said Bob. "Do you know any one of the name of Ruby?" "Why of course I do," said Bob, the colour rushing to his face, "but she ain't in there." "Yes, she is, or says so." "He's got her. Ods Daggs ! " suddenly exclaimed Bob. "Got her. Well, who?" "Don't go talking like that. What do you mean? Tell me, or I'll--" _ _

"Come, young man, you're a bit hasty. I shall have you up for—" "Say it again. Is Miss Ruby up there? Is it true, sir? Just save her; she don't want to be. I've been here every day and never seen her. What an idiot I am!"
There was no mistaking Bob's tone. He was in earnest, and in a dreadful fright. "What have you come here for this morning?" said the slim man.

"I'll tell you, if you'll help her. Oh, she'll be just going out of her mind, if she's with that man." "So you know something about it! I thought you were an accomplice." "I'm nothing but Bob, and if you help her, I know someone as'll give you a whole soy. He offered me one, but I don't care to be paid. Ain't a swell mob. Daresay now that you are." The man laughed. "Ain't time to laugh. Are you going to help her or not? [low did you get that?" "It was dropped at my feet out of the window." "Oh, he's awful deep. It's no use going and asking. Look here, if you wants to earn that soy., just you stay here, and I'll go and see what's up, and come and tell you. The man thought a minute, then he said: "Not a bad idea. Tell me what you know." "Miss Ruby's the squire's daughter—him yon asked me about in the train; I remembers you, though you cuts me. Well, she won't be made to marry Mr. Ji mes. She cut and run, but he's awful cute; he's found her, and not told the squire, I'll bet." "Very well you go and tell me. Don't stay too long. Will he listen to you?" "I've brought him a piece of news he wants to hear." "What's that ? " "Never mind. I'll go and see." Bob rushed off, and the man in the great coat looked after him till he saw him enter the house.
"Is that boy all right? I thought he was one of the crew."

He went down a passage, and found a policemttn waiting for him. "All right. Come as near as you can; I think we'll get one of them to-day. They have the girl. Just found her, I think—l don't know how or where. When I whistle, run him in." "All right, sir. But that boy is one of that lot. He comes here every morning." "I'm doubtful about him, but I know the girl there."

Bob had flown upstairs and knocked at the door. "Who's there ? " said James Felton's voice. "It's me, sir, got news for you." "Eh, news? Well, wait a minute." There was a little interval, Bob heard voices, but there were two doors. He could not be sure of it.
James came out on the landing. "I'm very busy—going away directly. Tell mi at once, and then take this note to the squire." "Mr. Alec is at the office, and he'll be coming out at one o'clock."

_ "Iltunph ! It never rains but it pours. Well, I must trust you to follow him to his lodgings, and come to the hotel and tell the squire." "All right, sir." ' "I may put off my visit, if I could catch him this evening. I declare, it is worth while. All right, now run with this letter; and here, Bob, if I don't see you again, here's a soy, for you." I "Thank you, sir; I was wanting one badly." "All right, now don't be late; off with you." Bob went off, but came back, hoping to see some- thing of Ruby, but James was watching him. "Shall I get you a cab, sir? Are you going soon?"
_ "Yes, call a cab, and tell it to wait." "Yes, sir."

• Bob went off delighted. Downstairs, however, he found no trace of the man with the great coat. He looked up and down the street, but in vain. "He's not wanting this soy.," said Bob, feeling very angry. He called a cab and told the drives that a gentleman was coming soon, and he was to wait for him. "I think I'd better wait too, but he'll be awful angry. He'll nigh kill me; but if it's to save Miss Ruby-- Perhaps it's all a make-up—a new trap set by the old gentleman." Bob was torn between conflicting thoughts, and he was also very angry with the man with the great coat for having made a fool of him. It was some time before anything happened. Bob was feeling bad, knowing that if James Felton saw him there would be something given to Bob which he would remember. But he said, over and over again to himself: _ - -
"Suppose it's true. Suppose Miss Ruby is there, and no one near to help her. He can only kick me or throttle me."

He looked round to see if he could hide himself, but he didn't wish to get too far away. If Miss Ruby wanted help, he'd fight for her, come what might. The waiting seemed terribly long to Bob; but at last there was a noise. The door opened, and jatnes Felton hurried out so quickly that Bob hardly realised what was happening. Yes, there was Miss Ruby! At the first moment she did not see Bob; indeed, not till he ran forward just as James had shut the door, calling out: "Drive on to Victoria Station." ! Bob!" cried Ruby. "Bob, save me I" Bob sprang on the step like a wild cat. James raised his stick, and struck the boy a blow—a blow which made him reel and fall heavily down under the wheel; but that moment's delay had given time to the man with the great coat to take Bob's place, and at the same instant a policeman seized the horse's head. "It was a dastardly assault," cried the man on the step. "Stop Stop!" , "Go on," cried James, "go on, cabman; I was assaulted by that boy. Go on, I shall miss my train. Ruby, sit still. Hands off Who are you ? " James was desperate. He raised his stick again, but at that moment the other door was opened, and Ruby was almost dragged out. She immediately began to run blindly forward. "Stop, miss; we want you. You must be a witness."

"No, no; let me go. I did nothing! I must get back. It's all true—Bob knows me." A crowd had gathered, and James's eyes looked dangerous. , Before the man in the great coat could call for more help, and whilst the policeman was firmly trying to stop Ruby, James made a desperate plunge, and actually slipped past everyone before he could be held back. •"Follow him," cried the man. "Leave the girl alone. What did you bother about her for ? " Ruby found herself alone, but seeing James's retreating figure at the bottom of the street, she stopped, for she suddenly remembered poor Bob, who was lying motionless against the kerb-stone, and no one Caving had time to pick him up. "Poor Bob! Oh, he saved me ! Please, do help him!" She turned her pale face toward,: the man in the great coat. "Yes, here is the owner of these lodgings. She will see to him. Will you tell me how long you have been in that house ? "

"Not long—at leas.t, I can't remember. It seems years, but it was only this morning. A, friend was ill; I went to fetch the doctor, and he saw me. Indeed, I was forced to go with him. Can't the law punish such wicked people? Ue said I was his wife. Indeed, it is not true ! " "I think your name is Miss Beauwo,th ? You sent me that message? It was fortuna;.e for you that I passed by and saw you in the act of making your presence known." "Oh, I thought I should never be saved," said Ruby, clasping her hands. "Poor Bob, let me go to his. Where is papa? I ought to let hini know I am safe; but I am so much afra'q of—that man!"

"Do not be afraid. Tell me, Miss Beauworth, where is your cousin, Mr. Alec Beauvrath, to be found? \Vo have been looking for him." Ruby looked puzzled. "You havo been looking for him? Do you mean that you---" "Don't be frightened. It is all for his advan- tage. Now, may I send you back to your friends?" "1 don't cnow what they will think of me! But, Bob, he is so good, so true, I must see him." At that moment the landlady came out of the house.
"The arm is broke, sir, and he's feinted. Ths youth had better go to the '9spitnt ; I ain't a-going to be the render-voos of the police, and s 9 I tell

you x aon t Know your name, sir, out you inter!, ferea with my lodger, as paid his bill with a cheque this very morning." "Very well. Here, boy, fetch a cab, and take lum to the nearest hospital. I will see to him, Miss aeauworth, but I will first conduct you honokn "No, no, go with him; I will go back to Mn. Vernon, if someone will get a cab." "Give me your address, and write this evening to me—Mr. Hansford. Does Dr. Murray know?" "Dr. Murray will never believe me. Oh, no, he knows nothing. He will think me so ungrateful. If you know him, will you tell him all about it? Mr. Hansford smiled. "I will tell him all I know. In the meanwhile, may I ask you one thing, Miss Beauworth ? Does Mr. Felton know Mrs. Vernon's direction?" "Yes, he found a letter addressed to me which dropped out of my pocket." "Ah, that is unlucky However, I don't think he will dare to come to you again." "Oh, I will not see him." He put her in a cab, as Ruby repeated: "And you will see that poor Bob is taken care of? I will ask if I may go and see him." Ruby drove off. She was still trembling, but the excitement kept her up. On the other hand, Mr. Hansford, as he called himself, went off to the hospital with Bob, and then took another cab and drove off at once to see Dr. Murray. Ile caught him just as he was going out. "Now, sir, we have a clue. But lam much afraid that Felton has escaped us. Still, he laid himself open to the law." He related the events that had taken place. "My poor little Ruby She will be ill. The shock will be very bad for her. I must go at once to Mrs. Vernon. You said she told you the old lady was ill." "You must try to find Mr. Beanworth, doctor. He is evidently hiding from Felton. He knows nothing about the young lady." "After all, this Bob was a hero, and you took him for a villain." "Yes, I own he took me in. Without him we should not have made sure of Felton. But, please, go; there is not a moment to lose. We must make sure the young lady is safe, for they will make another attempt to get hold of her." "But we are no nearer having proofs of what we want. Felton is a rogue, but we care nothing about him."
"If you will go to Miss Ruby-" "No; I think I will try and catch Mr. Beau- worth first."
"As you like, but then—then I will go imme- diately to Victoria.. He will try to get off at once."
(lb be concluded.)

The Death of Councillor Wilkinson.—Vote of
Condolence.

The MAYOR sail it was his m-lanchnly duty to move the following resolution : " That this Courici: receives with deep regret the announcement of the death of Mr. Joseph Wilkinson a Councillor of this borough, which took place on the 1$ inst., and desires to record the loss which the Council has sustained by his death ; and that the Town Clerk be requested to convey to the family of the late Mr Wilkinson their sincere sempatiay with them in their bereavement." Coacciller Wilkinson, he said, was known to all of them as a man of kindly and genial disposition, generous in thought as well as in act,always a friend of the poor, and as a membn• of the Corporation diligent and attentive to his duties, and possessed of all that patriotism which was so characteristic of Warring- ton people. He felt they had to some extent—all of them—lost a faithful colleague and a persona! friend. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Simms Feeanded, and said lve had known Councillor Wilkinson ail his life, and had always found him a most honourablis and upright man. He did not think he would be saying too much when be said that he was one of the most popular ward representatives in the Council. He was estesaned and r?spected. for his strict integritv and hone. t 7 of purpoie in all matters, asd althous.sh he was naturally of a modest and retiring disposition there was no member who was more sincere in his determination ts support only such measures as he considered were fsr the benefit of thetown. They would miss him very much. (Hear, hear.) The inotioa having keen carried, The MAYOR said : lam informed that it is very prob- able that tme name of Wilkinson will be maintained on the records of the Council, although I am anticipating in saying th,t But I think the suggestion is one that will be agreeable to us all if it turns out to be a fact. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were carried.

The Birth and Death Rate.
Serious Increase in the Infantile Death Rate.

Alderman SUTTON moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Health Committee, and said he was indebtei to the Medical Officer of Health for some impor- tant sta,tisties with referenc., `o the hirth and (ge tth rate of Warrington, for the year 1899. The statement read as fellows :—The number of hirths during the yrar was 2,309, the birth-rate being 36 07 per 1,000 of population, which is lower than any other year we have on record, and corresponds with the birth-rate of England and Wales, wWch is 29•3. The deaths rrgi.trerd durieg the year were 1,313, the death-rate bring 20 07 per 1,000 Df rennlation, the highest since 1892 and 1893, but one per 1,000 below the average rata in the ten years, 1889-98 The death-rate in England and Wales was 18.3,and in 33 great towns 20•2, and 67 other towns including War- rington! 18. The zymotic deaths were 322, and inclu- ded :—Scarlet fever, 29 • measles, 69 ; diphtheria, 7 enteric or teinhoid fever, 94 ; whooping cough, 34 •, and; diarrhcea, 159. The zvanotic death-rate w*s 503 per 1.000 as conapared with 221 per 1,000 in Eagland and Wales. Of the 159 deaths from diarrhce a 115 were under one year. The infantile death-rate was 194 per 1,000 births, or 26 above the average of the ten years 1889-98. Seven bundle-el and seven deaths were children under five years of age (or more than half of the total deaths), and of this number 449 were under one year. The report, continued Alderman SugToar, is not quite so satisfactory or eneeuraging as we could have wished, and the conclusion which may probably be arrived at in regard to the large'y-increased number of the deaths of infanta under one year will be that there must be greater negligence on the part of parents in the nursing of their chi'dren.
The MAYOR Secnnd9d, and the motion wan artreed to. The Central Depot at Parr-street.

The Paving and taking up of Streets.

He had head complaints from all quarters, arse' he echoed them. T' e. MAYOR : Are you referring ,to the electric cable ? Councillor BENNETT : Yes. _ The MAYOR: The work has to ho done twice—first relay'ng for temporary purposes whilst the material underneath gets set.
