div.head: EXAIVIINER, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 9 1900.
div.p: THE EXAIVIINER, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 9 1900.
The Proposed New Technical School. Statement by Councillor Monks.

At a meetine of the Museum, Library, Arts and Technical Instruction Committee a report on the pr posed new technical acho3l was under consideration. It was resolved that the report be adopted and forwarded to the Town Council, and that the sub-ceminittee pro- ceed to prepare instructions to architects. Mr. May ex- hibited specimens and drawings of the principal objects found during the excavations at Wilderspool in 1899. Councillor Morriss, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, ;aid the most important matter to which he wished to call attention was the report in connection with the proposed new technical school. He took it for granted that the Council were prepared to go forward with the school, because the sum of £15,000, which in his opinion was an inadequate sum, was included in the Bill which the Corporation obtained last year, and they could not now very well draw back. Another reason for going on with the work was that the commit- tee had had notice to quit the present buildines, the old barracks at the botsorn of Arpley-street. The Watala Committee wanted them out of there as soon as possible but, of course, it was out of the question, to think of removing at the present time be- cause there was no other suitable building in town, and it would take some time before the new building could be erected. With regard to the report itself, he did not know that he hetl much t 3 say; perhaps a more conveni- ent opportunity to discuss the school itself would be when they came forward with the plans and estimates, but the Sub-Conamittes had spent a deal of time in the consideration of the subject, and also in going about to several t owns, where new buildings had been put up, with the idea of seeing what other authorities were do- lase -nd as:f r as possible bon efitting by toeir expeeence. Tney toad men to St. Helens. Widnes, and Winstordeand Mr. Madeley had been to Stockport and Rochdale, and one or twe other places where there were new schools, to some extent, carrying on the work which the Museum Committee had to carry on in connection with technical instruction and secondary educatioe generally. The buildings proposed in the schedule were sufficient to provide for all the work that had been carried on during the last six or seven years and it should be remembered that they had had 900 students aed scholars for five or six years past—and in addition tney would provide new rooms such as a chemical Lahore- try, physical lecture theatre, &a., &c., in anticipation of what would be the requirements of the Education Department. The educational authorities were more and more insistieg upon practical work being done with the theoretical work. That was most desirable, and in view of the alterations which had been made quite re- cently, and others which were projected, and of which notice had been gi van, it was desirable these rooms should b eprovided. At present they could not state the dimensions of the rooms ; that was a matter that must to some extent be left with the architect. If the building was put up on the lines proposed it -yould give Warrington as good an institute as any town in the country possessed. The site had been settled upon, and it was between the Parr Hall and the Gymnasium, extending back into Museum- street, and as far as they could see it would appear to be desirable to have two entrances—one from Palmyra- square, which would be the front entrance and the entrance mainly:to the institute proper. By going into Museum-street a separate entrance might be got to be used for the Continuation Schools and else or two other departments separate and distinct from the Institute proper. There was no intention at present to go on with the establishment of a higher grade school, as the time was not quite iipe, but in the new institute they could make the necessary provision e ithout going 'into any additional expense. With regard to the pupil teachers' centre which it was suggested should be conductedfat the new Technical Institute, for some years batik the work of trainine, the teachers had been carried on under the direction of it voluntary committee,consisting mostly of school managers. That was satisfactory, but it was not an ideal arrangement, and in view of the additional regulati ins the D2partmeet was imposing it would be difficult to find in Warrinaton suitable accommodation to do that necessary work. Here, again, by careful consideration and planning they could provide for that teaching with- out addeienal expense. The classes in connection with a higher grade school and a pupil teachers' centre were conducted in the day time so that they would not inter- fere with the evening classes of the Institute. Then arose the question of the Assembly Hall, "in which,' to quote from the report, "prize distributions, general lectures, and similar functions might be carried on." It was not strictly necessary for institute purposes, but they had often felt the want of such a room in Warring- ' ton. In the interests of the Own it was desirable that such a hall should be built. They bad nothing in the town between the Parr Hall and the Co-eperative Hall which accommodated 500 people, and the one suggested might be very useful. Alluding to Mr. Mit, and the x- cevations at Wilderspool,Counciller Monks observed that the special thanks et the Council were due to him for the time and trouble he had bestowed on the matter. Pk was an enthusiast in this case., but it was very often the enthusiasts who did the most work. This was a case in point and his work deserved special mention. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR seconded the adoption of the minut es,and pointed out that he bad asked Mr. Monks to move their adoption because he had had so much to do w't s the preparation of the report in connection with the pro- posed new technical school. He cordially suppplrtecl the reference to Mr. Thomas May. It was, perhsps,not commonly known, but Mr. May had already sent t ) the Museum a considerable number of the articles which had been found at Wilderspool. The whole of his" finds" were ultimately to find their way into the Museum (Hear, hear.) He had bon the means of discovering the condition of things relating to times lone gone which were of permanert interest to the town and district. Councillor BENNETT wished in the first place to ecko the remarks which road been made by Coancillor Minks and the Mayor to Mr. May's valuable services to the town. The public were now beginning to realize his valuable services to the town. With regard to the pro- posed new technical school he su.ggested the acceptence of the following amendment :—"That the sub-commit tee prdeeed to prepare instructions to architects, and to request them to consider the possibility of utilising the land in Museum-street, leaving the space between Parr Hall and the Gymnasium open for possible future development." Thu MAYOR ruled the amendment out of order. Councillor BENNETT : Not tht observations?

The MAYOR: No,, but tie amendment is certainly out , of order, because any alteration to the report must come from the committee who present it. You will be in order in makingany observation on the report consistent with your views. Councillor Beene= then alluded to the two industrial exhibitions which had been held in Parr Hall, and to the annexe which it had been found necessary to put up. A third exhibition cf a similar character was stiortly to he held, and the space between the two buildings was to ao connected again. He had a strong opinion that the land between Parr Hall and the Gymnasium might be devoted to a more appropriate use than was now intended. He admitted that we Lad many irons in the fire at the pre- sent moment, but at some future time they might cever over the land between tee Hall and the Gymnasium and meet something in the shape cf what was familiar to some—that prosperous and flourishing building in the Cast elael or London.the People's Palace. That part of the town ought to beset apart for amusement and recreation and there need be no interference with the Technical Institute. He had no desire to cripple the institute, and if he had thought what he had suggested would do so he would not have mentioned the matter. No one was more anxious to see the institute thoroughly equipped than he was, but there was room in Museum-street for all technical instruction purpsses. They might link the fcur buildines together, and make them week in a sort of union. (Hear, lifer.) Councillor Monies said that Councillor Bennett, in pursuing his ideas showed an amount of perseverance which he could admire, and his only regret was that he pushed his motives to such an unwarrantable extent. The matter had been discussed by the sub-committee in the first ease, then Councillor B nnett put his views be- fore the Museum Committee, and in neither case did he find a seconder, and it was, therefore, unfair that he should bring before the Council a matter that was for the committee pure and simple, This was not the only occasion in which he had made the mistake of not acceptire the ruling of the committee. In the speaker's opinion it wan a matter of import- apes, and would be an advertisement to have the principal entrance to the building in front of the street, open to the public, was when the, 84W the elec- tric light which would be used they would ask what the bu 'ding was for and what benefit it would cenfer. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were then agreed to. Improvements at the Cemetery Chapels.

At a meeting of the above corn olittee it was res )led that the Borough Survey or advertise for tenders for the erection of a screen across the Church of England Chapel, the re-tiling of the floor, the erection of an oc.tere doo to the portico, and the friday of new swing doors according to the I,lan produced, and that the Bo eueh Sw:veyzr obtain tenders for the fiqing up of fireplaces with besting apparatus and the rLmoving of the stoves in the chapels. Councillor JOHN EVANS in moving the adop' ion of the minutes referred t the first resolution, and amended it to refer to the three chapels. The screen, he slid, would be confined for the preseat to C.s. Church of Eceand chapel, and the object o-. the committee in asking for that was to have a separate chamber for the reception of the c ffin during the service. Ti,is would ebviato scenes of some unpleasantness such as they had had in the past. Councillor tr. JOLLEY seconded.

Alderman SUTTON sail he was plea,ed to see that the committee were abut to do somt.thing to improve these c'oapels, for they were shout the coldest places in exist- ence. He would recommend, however, that instead of retiling with the present cldsFi of tiles a wooden floor should be substituted. Tint would he much more com- fortable and better in every respre• It was very de- sirable that the heating should be improved. I was quite evident that the stoves did not act as they should and that proper hat-ing apparatus ehould be substituted.
There had be.en complaints flr a long number of years

ICouncillor MONKS said he had some observations to make as the result of represeatations by a minister who usA the Nonconforanist chapel, bct the amendment of the minutes removed the groued for his remarks. With regard to the fixing of the screen he did not consider it necessary to do it as an experiment, becauie the same thing had been done all over the country in nlw ceme- tery chapels anti in many old ones the alteration had been made. The experience of warrington was the ex- perience of other towns, and they had carried out what Warrington now proposed to do. The three chapels might just as well be included now. (Hear, hear.) There had b,eu complaints of the conduct of people at the cemetery doting funerals and he thought a uniformed man might be employed there. The Corporation might have a man in their employ suitable for the capacity. A jc.lo of this kind would do instead of pensioning a work- man off. He was further of the opinion that the chapels might be made pleasanter by the use of some of the flowers from the greenhouses. The Mit.YOR said the Council would support the com- mittee in anything they considered reasonable to provide for the more comfortable accommodation of those who had to go there awl anything which might make the place less dangerous than it was at the present time on cold days. _ _ _

Councillor EVANS said it was the intention of the corn- ml;" 'e to make the chapels brighter and moreicomfort- able. Councillor Monks suggestion would be brought before the committee and he had no doubt it would be adopted. With regard to Alderman Sutton's suggestion abeut having a wooien pavement, the committee had already considered the matter and found that they would not be suitable in the chapels. Übe minutes were then confirmed, The Turkish Baths.—An Elaborate Scheme. A•.; a meeting of the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Oemtnittee it was resolved "That the plans marked • A' for the erection of Turkish baths, the alteration of the second-class bath and the ladies' bath, and the re- construction of the slipper baths, be approved. That the Electric Lighting Committee be requested to provide the following building; with wires and fittings for elec.• tric lighting, viz, :—The Town Hall, Bank House, the Public Baths."

Alderman Borrow, in proposing the confirmation of the minutes, said it was time this baths scheme was completed. In the first place, some years ago it was agreed that the baths were quite inadequate and that a first-class swimming bath was necessary. A first-class swimming bath was provided. The slipper baths were quite inadequate now, and there was a growing demand tor Turkish baths. The scheme now presented was most suitable and satisfactory. They had made the best arraneements possible on the vacant land at their dis- posal. Re produced plans and read the following repo* of the architect (Mr. T. Beesley) : Additions—Turkish' baths. The new entrance will be in Bath-street and on the right of this will be the cooling room or divan, about 38 feet square : accorxtodation provided for about 15 people. It will be lighted with side windows and top light, and fitted up with lounges and dressing rooms, divided by curtains or wood screens. There will be a plunge bath 30 feet long, six feet wide, and four and a half feet deep. Three hot rooms are arranged. First will be 36 feet long by 16 feet wide heated to 140 degrees. Second, 20 feet long by 13 feet wide heated to 180 degrees. Third, 13 feet long by ten feet wide heated to 280 degrees. There will be three steps up to the latter and the hating chamber below. The suite of hot rooms will enable the bather to vary the heat to suit his constitution or comfort. A shampooing room 20 feet long, ten feet wide,fi:ted up with modern improvements also a douche room, with needle douche, shower, spinal shower, and ae‘cencling shower. A small room- for the attendant with a room for towels. &c. Provision can be made for a smoking and coffee room. The basement would contain workshop, stores, coals,heating apparatus &c. The lighting by gas or electric incandescent light, special attention to be given to the ventilation and sanitary departments. Alterations—lt is proposed to have one general entrance in Bath-street in elder that the adminiltratiens may be better arranged and facilitate the working. By this means better access will be obtained to all the swimming, private and Turkish baths. A manager's house is shown on the plan to the left of the entrance. The alterations and improvements to the old buildings consist of building 16 new private 'oaths, and altering the old second class baths. The old private baths are considered unfit, and a new series should be fitted up in connection with a main c-rridor six feet wide. The ladies' swimming bath will be entered from the left of the corridor, and the boys' bath at the end of the corridor. The space now occupied by the private baths will be utilizsd for the enlargement of the boys' swimming blth and the extension of the boiler house, which will be necesiary by the enlargement of the baths. The old entrance to the first ciao swimming bath might be retained,to be used as an extra exit when entertainments are given. The Alderman added that the committee were unanimous in recommend- ing the scheme, which would cost about £5,000 though the Turkish baths themselves would only cost about £2,700. It was intended to fit the whole place up witta the best materials, as they thought any other me- thod would be false economy. The Turkish baths, Alderman Roberts added, would cost about £3,000. and the whole scheme could be carried out for about £5,000. No or was the time for the whole scheme to be carried out, and there was a guarantee that it would prove pro- fitable. The corn;nitteeelead agreed to the scheme MlARi- mously. Couecillor Dr. CANNELL seconded.

Alderman SUTTON said he thought ha asked a question in c-nimittee as to whether it would not he better in the first instance to build only what was sufficient for the purpose. The spending of £5,000 seemel to him to be a large order. At the present time they did not know howl these baths would be supported. He thought a commencement might be made with a small bath,which ef)uld be supplernent-d if found necessary. He asked the committee t take some further opinion on the matter. _

The MAYOR thouaht Alderman Bolton had made it clear that the Turkish baths were only to cost £2,700. The teat was for necessary alterations and improve- ments. Alderman BOLTON, ha reply, said it would be a false economy to carry out the scheme piecemeal. The minutes were approved. Markets Committee. Mr. Place's Salary.

At a meeting held on January 22ad it was resolved that the salary of Elijah Place, as inspector of weights and measures, be increased by £lO per annum and that the Electric Lighting Committee be requested to provide the market hall and sheds with wires ad fittings for electric lighting. Alderman HUTCHINSON in movinz the confirmation oF the winutes referred to the 33 years of excellent service rendered to the Corporation by Mr. Place, and said that he quite deserved the increase. Councillor ROGERS seconded, and it was carriel. Gas Committee. Labourers and Their Wages,

At a meeting held on January 12th, the engineer re- ported that the labourers had asked for an advance in their wages from 5J to 543 per hour,and after considera- tion it was resolved that the Chairman and Deputy- Chairman meet the men at an early date to discuss the question. The engineer was instructed to advertise for tenders for the decoration and furnishing of the new offices at Longford. Alderman FAIRCLOUGH moved the adoption ef the minutes In reference to the dispute with the employees, he said they had refusld to meet the chairman and deputy-chairman, and there the mattter ended. Alderman BOLTON seconded, and the minutes were agreed to. The Fire Brigade. Superintendent's Annual Report.

The minutes of the Fire Engine Committee contained the annual report of Mr. F Turner, the superintendent, which is as follows :—I beg to present the annual report of fires in Warrington and District for the year enaing December, 1899. The total number of " calls " was 21, a decrease of five on the previous year. There was one serious fire in the borough, the others being only slight. Two serious fires occurred outside the borough, one of these being on a steamer in the Latchford Looks. The total damage was £6,241, a decrease of £15,227 on the previous year. The damage in the borough was £4,305, a decrease of £13,063, the bulk of which was caused by the damaAe at Messrs. Barker's fire in Haydoek-atreet. The damage eutside the borough was £1,933 a decrease of £2,164 on the previous year. Our services wore not required at five fires, the small steamer " Major was used at five fires, the large steamer " Captain" at two fires, hydrants were used at seven fires, and one fire was extinguished wi• h buckets. There was one false alarm. There were 4,050 yards of hose used in extinguithing the above fires. ' The attendance of the firemen at fires during the year has been very good, an average of over 15 men at each fire. Thu monthly practices hare been well attended. I hr vn inspected the fire appl'ances at the various public buildings during the year, and found theirs in good working order. The strength of the brigade is 21 officers and men, two steamers and one manual engine, 10 standpipes, keys, and four-ladders on truck, one 60ft. fire escape, one 40ft. combined hose and curricula fire escape, two hand pimps, with 1,600 yards of unlined canvas hose, in good condition 9 and two hand reel carts, Causes of fire : Unknown, 10 ;in contact with light 4; 'sparks, 1; overheating, 2 ; chemical explosion. 1: defec- tive construction, 1 ; false alarm, 1 ; total 20. Places of fire : Farms, 7 ; dwelling houses, 3 ; cabinet works, 2 ;be stead works, 1; lodging house, 1 ; laundry, 1 ; rubber works 1 ; drying room, 1 ; chemist's store, 1; fittins- and pattern shop, 1 ; steamer, 1 ; false alarm, 1. 1 have to thank the Chief Constable and the police under him for the assistance they have given eviler' rsevired. The horsing of the engines has been smartly attended to by Mr E Connor, Sankey-street, Councillor TINNIO7 propo3ed cho ado ..tion of the miautes, which was carried. Rivers Committee. The Widnes and Runcorn Bridge Bill.
The Rivers CommLtee at a meeting held on January 22nd resolved that a petition be presented against the
Widnes and Runcorn Bridge Bill. The minutes were approved, OR the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Alderman MITCHINSON.
Electric Lighting. The Charges for Wiring.

The following resolutions were adopted as the ch.rges for lighting various meetings of the Electric Lignting Committee :—That the General Purposes Committee be requested to petition against the Lancashire Electric Power Bill; that the several committees having charge of corporate buildings be requested to censider the advis- ability of lighting the same with electricity, and of hand- ing the same over to this committee for the purpose of being fitted up ; that the committee do not see their way to adopt any system of free wiring,and that in their opinion it is advisable that intending consumers should make their own arrangements for the wiring of their premises. The Town Clerk reperebd that the Local Government Board had sanctioned the borrewing of the sum of £44,966 for the purposes of electric lighting. Councillor Moreirs in proposing the confirmation of these minutes asked for the inclusion of one relating to the charges, a matter which was eliminated from the minutes of the last Council. With regard to the system of free wiring he explained that the term was a mis- nomer. They were not going to do anything for nothing. (Laughter.) It was better called wiring on the hire-pur- chase system. With regard to the lighting it was pro- posed to charge 63 per unit for the first 1 hours per day per quarter and 3d per unit after that per day per quarter. To put it plainly 1361thours per quarter would have to be paid for at the rate of 64 per unit ; anything above at the rate of 31. That was an average of the charges made in this part of the country. In Manchester there was an all-round charge of 53, Liverpool 4d, Chester 40, Bury 63, and 34 after, Blackburn' the same, Blackpool 7d, and 23 after. Wallasey 64 and no reduction. They had taken 63 and 3d as being about the average on the recomme%iation of Mr Preece. their consulting electrical enginoer. The committee hoped after the first year to make a con- siderable reduction in the charges. The charge at first was proportionately high because the number of people who were willing to take the light was relatively small. There was a large cayital expenditure and they wanted an adequate return. Warrington was peculiarly conser- vative in many ways and it was just possible that cue. tomers might not come forward in a rush, but they might expect to have in two or three years a satisfactory number of consumers taking a considerable quantity. They hoped to make a reduction after the first year. With regard to wiring, some people who would take the light would not pay a lump sum for wiring which cost 15s or 20s per light. The wiring could, however,be done, and the cost paid in instalments over a number of years, or the cost might be repaid by charging so much more per unit for the lighting proper. One reason alleged for adopting that was that the committee would obtain more customers. The experience of other towns, however, was adverse to the adyigability of he committee undertaking the wiring. They felt it would be far better if they had nething to do with it, especially as in the application to the Local Government Board for money for the work they did not include any sum for the purpose. They therefore had no funds. The Local Government Board had not yet granted the borrowing of money for any such purpose, and there was a little risk in it. It seemed beet to let it entirely alone, and 1-ave such person free to make his own arrangements with the company who were able and willing to underteke the work. The Local Government Board had authorised the borrowing of the money for the general scheme and had not cut down the scheme in any way. That was entirely satisfactory, and they might congratulate themselves because it Was excep- tional. It spoke volumes for the work jdoue by Mr. Dees and Mr. Preece.
Alderman FAlecL3rtent seconded,and tbe minutes were agreed to.
The Equipment of the Volunteers.

At a meeting of the General Partwes Committee it was resolved that the Mayer be authorised to pay out of the Walker's Gift Account such sum as he and the Transvaal Relief Committee may consider necessary for the proper equipment of the Warringtoo Volunteers who have been accepted for active service in South Africa. The following recommendations of the Op mi Spaces Committee were approved :—That the wall in front of the old burial ground in Si. James-street be taken down and re-erected along the river side of such burial ground; that the fence erected across Victoria Park be set back to the line shown on the plan submitted, and that such fence be continued along the river side and also along the western side of the enclosure; that the Town Clerk give notice that the portion of the park so enclosed will be opened to the public after March 31st next; that the recreation ground in Howley be offered for sale by public auction.
The MAYOR moved the confirmation of tha committee's minutes.
Alderman FRiNCOMB seconded.

UnCißOr BENNETT asked whether the Corporation in- tended providing another open space at Howley in sub- stitution of the one it was proposed to sell. He would also like:to know whether the proposed new bridge across the Mersey at H ,wley had been definitely shelved. The MAYOR in reply said the money realised from tbe sale of the open space could only be applied for a similar purpose. In regard to the bridge it was felt that the present was an inopportune moment for bringing it for- ward.
Councillor BENNETT : Have the Corporation another open space in view? The MAYOR : Yes there is an alternative open space in the same district.
The Paving of Wilderspool Causeway and Knutsford-road. Strong Complaints.

Councillor JAMES Everss in accordance with notice of motion called attention to the paving of Wilderspool Causeway and Knutsford-road and afterwards moved a resolution thereon. He remarked that Wilderspool Causeway bad been left in a very awkward and slovenly condition for a long time, presumably with the object of waiting until the Corporation were in a position to lay down the tram lines for the electric tramways, but new that they were within measurable distance of having tramways the Paving and Sewerage Committee had de- cided to commence the paving of the street. He did not understand the action of the committee for it was certain that the road would have to be pulled up again when the tram lices were laid. There had already been a delay of eighteen months in paving the Wilderspool Causeway and he did not see why they could not wait a little longer and proceed with the paving after the tram lines had been laid. Since he came into the reom he had had a plan placed before him showing him where the tram lines were to be laid and he was certain that if the Corporation proceeded to pave the caueeway in a short time the setts would have to be pulled up again in the centre of the road in order ta lay the tram lines. He did not like this idea of doing work twice oder. (Hear, hear.) He thought this con- dition of things was due to a misunderstanding between the various committees of the Corporation. As soon as a street was completed it was almost certain that it would be taken up again for the purpose of laying pipes. If there were a working agreement between the com- mittees such a cendition of things could be avoided. As a member of the COULIC111:0 (id not like to be twitted at by outsiders about these things. The ratepayers' money was being wasted by the Corporation in doing work twice over when there was no necessity for it. When work had been doao well once that ought to be sufficient. (Hear, hear.) He was of opinion that for the Corporation to pave Wilderspool Cause way with setts: in view of the approaching tramway system would be a misappropriation of the ratepayers' money. With respect to Knutsford-road, he dare.a.y it was over zwelve months since he noticed some of the Corporation Workmen fixing hurdles near Victoria Park. At the present time the hurdles were still there, but the work had not been finished. He thought the Corpo ation was going to take down the wall and widen the road at that point. The proseet condition of things was very u:satis- factory. Work was commenced and left unfinished. They never know when it was going to ba complet 4. and if such a slip-shot condition of affairs existed at any private estatlishment somebody would be brought to hook. It wes time somebody said something about the matter and something was done to remedy the present condition of things. (Hear, hear.) He would propose a ' resolution "That Knutstord road and Wilderspool Causeway be not paved until such time as the tramways have been laid."

The MAYOR suggested that a better resolution would be tho following :—" That it be an instructi m to the Paving and Sewerage Committee to proceed only in such a manner with the pavement of Wilderspool Causeway and Knutsford-road as is consistent with the laying of tramways." Councillor EVANS decided to substitute that for his resolution. Councillor ELLisoN seconded.

Alderman FRANCOMB 6aid if by waiting a few more months the Corporation would be in a p3sition to lay down the tram-lines on Wilderspool Causeway it would be better to wait. But if the tramways were to be introdueed at SOM9 in iefinite tima they ought to pave the _road at once. (Hear,.hear).

alderman BOLTON said there was a heavy traffic on Wilderspool-road, and when new roads were made the crown generally gave way a littie. He did not see bow they could lay down the tramways at the present time. He sympathised with the remarks made abut the manner in which the roads were continually being pulled up, and he thought it would be better if the Committees concerned would meet together and arrange to lay all piper requirea at the game time. (Hoar, bear). Councillor TrsNioN said in the absence ot the Chair- man and Deputy-Chairman of the committee he had been asked to read the following correspondence, which would explain what was being done in the matter and perhaps save discussion "February 2nd, 1900. Dear Sirs,Warrington Tramways For over twe years Wialarpaal and Latchford Cause- ways whpre the tramways are proposed to be run have been ordered to be paved, but owing to the laying of c..rtsio gas an.l water mains, and the difficulty of pro- curing material the work ha a been delayed: We have had seriou3 complaints in reference to the state of the road and having had the material for the greater portion

of the paring my committee instructed me to proceed with the work. I find that a member of the Council has given notice of motion to have the paving stopped until such time as the tramways are laid. This will cause great delay and considerable expense particularly as the setts are lying on the ground and the interest on them will be considerable. I think it is quite possible to go on with this paving and so work the setts that when the time COMEN for laving the rails that a portion of them can be taken up for the insertion of the rails. I enclose you a section of how I propose to do this if it meets • your approval. In the first place I will put down the six inches of concrete to receive the tram lines and allow for five inch setts. I would suggest that we pave the road to within a foot of the intended new tram lines as shown on the plan, and in the foot space on each side of the rails I would pave the setts longitudinally so that when the rails are to be laid the setts can be taken up and the rails :aid in on the concrete. I think the plan will suffi- ciently explain itself and I should be glad if you would kindly say whether you can do with less that a foot on °Jen side of the rails. When the rails are laid of course we should pave the setts into the cross paving in the usual way. I should be glad if you would reply to this letter per return as it is important that I should have your reply for the committee meeting on Monday next. —Yours faithfully Thomas Longdin, Messrs. Preece and Cardcw, 13, Queen Ann's Gate, Westminster." Messrs. Preece and Cardew replied as follows :—ln reply to yours of the 2nd lust, we do not see any objec- tion to paving the Wilderspool and Latchford Cause- ways as shown on drawing enclosed with your letter. We presume you have a copy of the deposited plans which shows position of lines, passing places, and width between centres of the tracks. We should like to have an opportunity of fully discussing with you the details, before the work is actually put in hand." Councillor TINNION, continuing, said the committee approved of what the Borough Surveyor proposed, and they were advised that the job would be quite as firm and good as if the lines were not there at all. He thought it would be a mistake to stop the work. Couucillor BENNETT said before they put down any tram-lines it was necessary to decide whether the electric traction was to be by the overhead system or by the conduit system. Alderman HUTCHINSON said the causeway aould be partly paved without interfering with whatever system was adopted. Alderman SUTTON expressed his full sympathy with some of the speakers as to the enismenagement of the roads generally. For many years there had been very serious complaints about the paving of streets and the repeated taking up of them. The MAYOR: lam afraid you are getting a little out- side Lite motion. Alderman SUTTON (continuing) exii he was not going to oppose the making of any streets but he was t)t opinion that a little more discussion between certain committees would prevent this continual taking up of streets. . . .

Aldermln FRANCOMB : That is not on the minutes. (Hear, hear.) Alderman SUTTON said he would take an esrly opp)r- tunity of referring to it. With respect to Wildersp )11 Causeway complaints were continually being made about its bad condition. _ _

The MAYOR said the [resolution did not cast any re- flection on the Paving and Sewerage Committee but on the other hand it would strengthen their hands and comp,l them to confer with the reF•pmsible engineers ie connection with the tramways and adopt such a plan as would prevent the possibility of the work being done twice over. The Tramways Committee had not yet decided whether they would adopt the overhead or under-ground system. At a meeting held only last week to receive the rnpresentative of the Nerthwich Light Railway they were told that the under-ground system had been adopted in such a manner as to make it possible for them to use it, and Mr Scotter was of opinion that the Corporation might also adopt it with a resonable prospect of success. The only argument had been the possible cost of the underground system as compared with the overhead system. That being the case the pro- posal which Councillor Tinnion had put before them so lucidly would at any rate have to be postponed until the system had been decided upon. A strmg foundation would be necessary for the tramway and if the underground system were adopted, accommodation would have to be provided for the system of traction. The objeet of the resolution was to enable the Paying and Sewerage Committe.•! to come to such an arrange- ment with those who were responsible for the tramways as to make it unnecessary to do the work twice ever. The provisional order would probably be granted in May. (Rear. hear.) Councillor F. R.Rozeirrs contended that the resllution as it had beea framed was weak, and it would be better to substitute the words " as will facilitate the laying of tramways "for the phrase " as was censistent with the laying down of tram lime" The MAYOR preferred the reading of the resolution. Councillor EVANS said he believed much good would result from the discussion. The resolution was unanimously carried. Re-Arrangement of the Seating Accom-

div.head: modation.
div.p: modation.

At the conclusion of the meeting the Mayor asked the opinion of the Council on the new arrangement of seats. These had been arranged in horse-shoe fashion with a passage down the centre. Several members expressed their approval of the alteration and it was deciled to try it again at the next Council meeting. The Council then rose.

div.head: SEQUEL TO A BETTING
div.p: SEQUEL TO A BETTING
TRANSACTION.
Claim at the Warrington County Court.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday morn- ing before his Honour Judge Gwynne James, Tbornas Green, greengrocer, Kouteford-road. Latchford; claimed from his uncle, Henry Green, £3 the winnings of a betting transaction. Mr. Browne, who appeared for plaintiff, said his client gave the defendant £2 to put on a horse. He put it on,it won, and he drew the money, £3 103. The same day he promised plaintiff that he would pay the amount when he received his annuity. Subsequently be refused to pay.

• ilis Honour agreed that the case was one which he could hoar. It wad, he said, a little outside the usual betting case. Plaintiff sued for money roccived in rela- tion to an illegal transaction. Defendant : The horse didn't win. (Laughter.).

• . . In answer to his Honour he stated that he received the £2 from the plaintiff to put on Mamppa, which ran in the Stewards' Cup at Goodwo3d Races last year. His Honour: Do you say Mazeppa didn't win? Defendant : Yes. Mr. Browne : Be said the same night that 119 drew £3los.

His Honour : I want to know whether Maz!ppa _won. (Laughter). Plaintiff said he gave defendant £2, to back £1 each way, and the horse ran third. The odds were 10 to 1 for a win, and 2i to 1 for a place. Defendant : I put the £2 on to win. His Honour: That disposes of it. Mr. Browne: He said the same night that ho would pay the money. His Honour : Where did you bet I'_ . . _

Defendant (after hesitaion) Battermarket- street. His Honour: To a man in the street? Defendant: No. At a house. His Honour : What Inuse ? The price are heregand will be interested to know. Defendant : The Pelican nublic-house. His Honour : Who was the bookmaker? Defendr.nt : I didn't know him. His Honour: Did you bet in the bar ? Defendant ; No. In ORP of the rooms. His Honour: __How many others were there?

Defendant: None. His Honour: Do you mean to tell me that you and the beokmaker had that room te yourselves on cup day? (Laughter.) Defendant : Yes. His Honour : You have bet before. Defendant : Never—(laught:-r)— with that man. Nis Honour: How came you to go into the back room of the Pelican if you had never bet before. Defendant: I heard there was a bookmaker there. Plaintiff came up five minutes before the race, and told me to put the money on. James Waterworn s tid he went with defendant to plaintiff's house after the race on the same day. Plaintiff said : " Well, its all right," and defendant replied " I cannot pay you now, becance I have parted with some of it. but I will pay when I receive my annuity. In answer to his Honour. Plaintiff said defendant had been with him at scares of race meetings. His Honour to (defeelant) : Have you never bet there ? Defendant: Yee. His Ilmuour : I thoueht you said you bad never bet before this ? Defendant . I said I had never bet before with that man. His Honour : Judgmeet for plaintiff for £3 10s.

WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.
Annual Meeting.

The annual meeting of the Warrington and District Agriniltural Society was hald at 23, Bald-street. on Monday afternoon Mr. H F Greenough presided over a good attendance which included tho Mayor, (Alderman Roberts), Captain Waring a.nci Messrs. J trues fi:Therd, Edward Gibbon, S Gould, Prieitner, J Shakeshaft, William Richardson, Tiasiey, T Charnock, Tickle, Weir, J Marsh, J Gould, Peter Dav!es, Colin Maclver (hon. secretary) and H. Beresford Mdville (secretary). FINANCIAL.

The SECRETARY read the E taem ent of acco,inta tor the past year which showed a i Icome of £335 163 lid to which must be ad3ed a sum of £5B 33 10.1 the balance in hand from 1898. The expenditure during the year wav £350 3s Bd, thus reducing the balauco in baud to £43 17e id.
Ttc accnunts were passed. ANNUAL REPORT,

The annual report which was read 117 the secretary stated that " The society, until lately known as the Warrington and District Mare and Foal Seeley, held its 10th annual show in Walton Park on August loth, by the kind invitation of the President, Sir Gilbert Grosse& ll Bart. There is no doubt that from all points of view the show was a success. Last year a clieme fer further ex- tension was sabmitted for censaieration by the thee existing Executive Committee, and was adopted by the menabsee at the annual meeting. It core:prised classes for cattle, cheese, butter, eggs, dressed poultry and potatoes. Competition was not excessively keen, but the entries give satisfaction oa the whole, considering the late hour at which the extension was iloated,and the restrictions contained in ttlr society's mules, which it may be consiuered desirable to alter in future, so as to Imp more in touch with the requirements of the district. Some slight alterations as to rules and con- ditions of ownerseip will be submitted for the due consideration of the members of tile annual meeting or at a specially called meeting for the purpese. Mr. Littleton Devrhurst, (of Lyrrina, kindly accepted the office of vice-president for the year. He preseated a very handsome challenge cup for the cattle clesses which certainly gave the society a ,ereat impetut in this di nw i vi- sion of the e exhibits. .It s a matter for regret that the shire classes for yearling, two year old and three year:old fillies were badly supported. As utile:there does not appear air explanation for this except that either in the trantitien state from foal to two or three years old the stock is not up to show loPri, or that the animals have been disposed of by the breeders. It is, however, hoped that breeders in the distriet will enter more largely in these particu:ar clews in the future as they are mot an encouragement to the committee at present. The draught gelding class,so far as number is concerned, was not as well filled as in pit Vi 1123 years, hut the exhi- bits, on the other band, were of a bieb wandard, and the judging of the class created a large amount of in- terest. Hunter and hackney class were quite up to the average both as to teem-tiers and quslity, but there is still great room for imprevement. Turning t ) the ad- ditional classes winch formed pir-. of the num scheme of this t ear'e show,the entries wee) not numeroue, Out el a good quality throughout. Ea. b class had a few exhibits, and the committee feel that they are fully joetified ia continuing the additional work now that the district rewises that such classes exist. The MAYOR, in reply. said he tbankqd the meeting very sincerely for the houour whicll had just been con- ferred on him, as he considered it an honour to be appointed to such a position. He (the Mayer) had come to the conclusion as an cut=iocr that if it paid a farmer to breed good horses, i p sin a merchant or a manufacturer to use god ones. THE EX.::,, M N EA?.
FEBRUARY 9Tri, 1900.
DR. LEYDS is said to be Is Intervention Probable? commencing vigorous efforts

to bring about foreign inter- vention between the Boer Rvublics and Great Britain. He gives out that he has a great sur- prise in stare for us when we have driven the in- vaders out of Natal. This attempt to discount approaching defeat is very clever, but it is hardly possible that it can deceive anybody who takes a sober view of the situation. The slight concessions Lord SALISBURY is making all round do not indi- cate any alarming disturbance in the diplomatic world. The French press is endeavouring to , stir up strife in Egypt, in which it is almost certain to fail. If there were any interests at stake we might have expected intervention before, . and nothing has occurred to make it more probable now than it was at starting. The American people, because they are Republicans, might be suspected of sympathy with the South African Republics. But they leave confined what sympathy is manifest to one or two limited demon- strations, and the protests against the detention of American cargoes to Delagoa Bay have had more reference to commercial intere3ts than to keen polit;.cal feeling. • President 11,143K1N. LEY has removed the late Consul at Pretoria be- cause he was evidently in the wrong place, and as he has since presumed to he a missionary of inter- vention he has been removed from the Consular list. France has no interests in Snuth Africa that are being imperilled, and the ground for any inter- vention on her part cannot be defined. We believe that the French Government, as such, will not move, much as the colonial party is seeking to create mischief by misrepresenting affairs to the Negus of Abyssinia and to embroil us with the Powers in Egypt. Russia will only act in the interests of France, and by way of diversion rather than of intervention. She has assisted France in obtaining an extension of the French concession in Shanghai, and Lord , SALISBURY has partly given way rather than keep open a cause of dispute. On her own part Russia has made a move in Persia, and she may yet make an advance:of some kind on the frontier of Afghan- istan. We have expected these minor difficulties,. but they are not intervention. in South Africa, and they do not:afford a basis for it. Germany is the only European Power in the least likely to feel that some of her interests may be adTected. But even Germany cannot desire ta see a strong mili- tary Power established in South Africa, with a frontier near to her, possessions, and able to com- pete successfully with Great Britain. The impres- sion is that Germany has been reconciled . to our action, and that the understanding is of a material character, involving territorial concessions. Had Germany been averse to. what we were meditating, she would have said so. The truth is that the time which is indicated as the intervention point shows that a political move only is ?ossible on Dr.. LEYDS' part. If the invaders of British territory are pushed back to their own country,. and they have then to repel an invasion, what possible ground can it give for intervention by Germany, , Russia, France, or America Persons who make. war must take the conseqgences, and. the Boers. , destroyed their hope for intervention when they deliberately became the aggressors and pro- ceeded to annex, in form, what was not their own. They must suffer for their folly.
IF it should come to be. The Nicaragua thought that the United: Canal.

States had taken. advan- tage of our embarrassments to obtain the abroga- tion of the canal clauses of the Clayton-Bulwer Treaty there would. be some feeling of resentment at such unfriendly conduct. But it is satisfactory to learn that the negotiations began before, the South A.frican War, and that they have been matured in Washington, owing te% the untiring efforts of Mr. HAY, who represented the late American Government in London. This country gives up its rights over a pos9ihie canal through Nicaragua, and obtaina nothing whatever in re- turn. The Americans will have to make the canal and manage it, but the canal itself will be open to all the world, and it cannot, become a theatre of operations in war time. Whether the Americans will find the money and begin an entirely new canal is by no means certain, but it is Row possible or the operation to be commenced and carried out, in which case the works on the Panama Canal, now arrested for want of money, would be entirely abandoned, and Frenchmen would have lost all the money they

have subscribed for the undertaking. Such a con- tingency has to be faced, and it involves interest- ing paints. Two canals are not required, and they would not pay. But the possession of the right to construct a canal north of the one some- what advanced may make the French subscribers willing to sell their undertaking for a moderate sum of money, which could ha easily raised in the United States,along with whatever may be needed to complete the enterprise. In any case, the ad- -vantage will be with America, and it will not con- duce to the improvement of the relations between the United States and France already less cordial than they used to be, in consequence ot the attitude Franca adapted during the war in Cuba. The good understanding between America and this country ought to be very materially increased by the new evidence of good- will which we have given. It is a surrender which costs us nothing, if we gain no practical concession by means of it. The right was a shadowy one, 'and it was not worth retaining at the risk of any temicon between the two countries. No British capital would be forthcoming to make a canal through Nicaragua, with the probable trouble with America it would be likely to cause sooner or later. A canal is needed, and it is much better that it should be made with American capital, especially

now that the Americans are expanding their ' --- ideas with regard to an external policy,territorial as well as political. How far the growth of American influence in the Gulf of Mexico may affect the future of our West Indian islands cannot now be determined, and at some distant date we may be sure that questions will atise involving the assertion cf American rights over every island in the group, unless some reaction should occur, of 'which there are at present no indications. Round- ing off possessions is likely to become a pretty general policy in the years to come, and whenever the Americans desire to acquire rights over all the islands contiguous to their southern mainland we may be quite sure that some excuse will be found for making a bargain with us about the West Indies. The more gradual the acquisition of them the better, but we think it is bound to come with- in the next hundred years, either after or before the Central American States have been embraced Within the scope ot the United States.

It is, perhaps, fortunate that the threatened discussion on Ritualism will not form a part of the debate on the Address in the House of Commons. Subject only to the consideration of the conduct of the War in the past, members and the people of the country generally are eager to hear Mr. Wyndham's statement as to proposals for strength- e„ning our military system; and, in the fitness of rings, an announcement of this sort should not be delayed by a discussion regarding legislation in 50nle future session. The party who desire a stricter discipline in the Church must be aware that they have to arouse enthusiasm among a body of men who are not conspicuous for zeal in religious controversy. Many of these, too, would not vote for any motion to stir up the Government in this affair, except under pressure from their constituents ; and their constituents are far too occupied now with the war to make any large movement. The demonstration at the Albert Hall last week may be cited in opposition to this theory, but it would be a small compliment to the combative portion of the Low Church party to say they could not fill this building, spacious as it is, with adherents at any time. It is not by such a rallying of their forces that they can expect to gain their point, but by provincial meetings in the small centres, in the hearts of the constituen- cies. Without touching the arguments, therefore, it may be said that Mr. &tame' Smith may be glad that his amendment has not any immedi Ito Prospect of coming before the House. Moreover, the Bishops have given a collective promise, by the utterance of the Primate and the Diocesan of London, to do their best to put their house‘in order. These prelates, at any rate, are held to be the mouthpieces of the private council held by the Wearers of lawn sleeves on the subject. They Will, in the breathing space,have an opportunity of testing their influence on the clergy in thpir care.

York election result is only a small disappoint- ment to the Liberal party though it is a big and Portentous event in Conservative eyes. Perhaps it could hardly be expected that Mr. Murray should succeed where Sir C. Furness failed, but had the contest been a purely political one there would have been a large amount of confidence in the Liberal nominee nevertheless. But the contest though fought by politicians of opposite beliefs, factor in was not a political contest. The war was the main the fight, and in the result too. The nment candidate had a strong card—or a succession of strong cards—in the war, notwith- standing the blunders of those in office. Those blunders are past, the prospect is now more hope- ful, and Mr. Faber was both able and willing to strike loudly on the chord of patriotism. Electors were warned not "to be deserters at the poll in this the hour of your country's need," and there can be no doubt at all that many Liberals sunk their political leanings in a desire not to further ernbarass the Govornrnent. Yet it is a significant fact that in this hour of national peril nearly 5,000 electors voted against the party in Power. There is no indication whatever of any weakening of Liberalism in the constituency,and we doubt not that when a real trial of party strength "rues—as it must soon—the " party of progress" Will win the day. As things are now, one can only congratulate Mr. Murray on his plucky fight against odds, and sympathise with him in his defeat.

-- The remarkable statements made by Mr. Wynd- lam, the Under-Secretary for War, in the House Of Commons last Thursday will 'go very far towards re-assurina the people of the British Empire. We thought the representatives of the daily press had kept a sharp eye on the number of men going out to South Africa to fight for the Queen and country, but they have been consider- ably . wide of the mark in their estimates. Mr. Wyndham tells us that within two or three weeks the British Army in South Africa will exceed 180,000 men—a truly colossal tetra. About 150,000 , was the highest unofficial estimate, and it is decid- edly comforting to learn that we shall have quite 30,000 more men to fight our battles than we expected. The strength of the Colonial forces has been one cause of the public misapprehension. These valuable volunteers have been enrolled they actually here, there mil everywhere until number 33,000. Over 7,000 are Canadian and Australian, the rest being South African. The fact, too, thmt our mounted troops are nearly 40,000 strong is entirely a new one, and adds to the general feeling of reassurance which Mr. Wyndhani s speech has caused. The Boers Probably number 60,000 men, with 110 guns, and against this force we are able to nut 180,000 men With 452 guns. Can it be doubted,that with odds of three to one, the tide will turn in our favour Soon? We think not.

It will probably be interesting news to Warring- tonians that the world actually contains some Worse roads than thise which intersect this ancient borough. China is the country favoured by these remarkable thoroughfares, which we are told, were perfect some 2,000 years ago, but not having been repaired since, are a little bit bad. It is related of Lord Charles Beresford, When over among the Celestials, that he complained to a friend about the condition of the roads. The friend—a Yankee by the way—replied. " Yes ! the roads are bad. There was a mule drowned in the road. outside my em- bassy the other day !" After tins we feel safe in counselling patience among Warrington wheelmen

div.p: and others, for it is not quite 2,000 years since the roads were repaired, nor have they yet sunk so low as their Chinese relatives.

Penketh people being possessed of sensitive olfactory nerves have instituted a campaign against the depositing of manure on the banks of the Mersey. They do not like the smell of manure, especially after it has stood for a while and ripened, and they are determined not to endure it. The Parish Council acting on their behalf, tried to move the District Council in the matter, but that body proved too lethargic or unwilling, and the result was aggravating. With commend- able persistency the Parish Council stirred up the County Council,which duly issued a mildly-phrased mandate to the District Council;and at last some- thing has been done. The aforesaid lethargic District Council discussed the question, but showed no desire to abate the nuisance. They would like to have believed Mr. Houghton's statement that the manure did not smell after it had lain for " a month or two," but Mr. Dignum spoke out vigorously for the Penketh residents, and it was ultimately decided to allow the manure to remain a fortnight. Probably the nuisance will be as great as ever. We never yet found manure which failed to assert its presence, whatever its age or youthfulness. The District Council how- ever, is not disinterested ; it has rather a liking for manure, and the Penketh people will have to be very determined indeed before they get what they want and what they are entitled to.

RUNCORN NOTES. [BY A COREWSPONDENTI "Regularity, diligence anl success is put into one side of the scale by the industrious scholar, and at the year's end, the School authorities put into the other Bide a 4-id book. What mockery! But that is not the wont which may be sail about the atter, for the "4I worths" that have been handed to the" regular, diligent, and successful" as a full and sufficient reward are but the resultant of an enterprising firm's advertising acumen, and probably cost the School Authorities little or nothing.

At the meeting of the School Board,last Thursday week, some very interesting figures were given us, and a method shown, by which diligent and pains- taking parents might save the town about 21. in the rates. The whola town appreciates the fact, but while doing so,it is not out of place to call attention to the monstrosity in connection with the recent distribution of prizes to the scho:ars attending Victoria-road Board School. It does not matter to us whether the books were purchased or nftt for nothing, as prizes they are absolutely valueless, and hold out little or no inducement to a scholar to continue "regular, diligent, and success- ful." Rather let the !prizes be few and far between and of some value; than absolutely priceless, and a mockery!

Conscription, we are told, has been relegated to a back seat; and se far as Runcorn is concerned it is not likely to be again referred to Some short time ago Captain Ashton of the "F" and "Cr Com- panies, 2nd, E. Ches. Vol. Batt*, asked for recruits. Last Saturday night he told us he had "got them." and that the recruiting this year was fully 200 per cent better than in any Year since his connection with the movement. This i but the illustration of what is taking place all over the country,and whilst this spirit prevails there is little fear of Us becom- ing acquainted with that ugly word which is far too continental for our insular palates.

There have been many meetings of the learned rescting the formation of a Tradesman's Associa- tion for our town, and I have been given to under- stand that at length a move will be taken by that hitherto " invisible body" to make itself known to all and sundry. The sine-qua-non of membership is said to be : a bona fide tradesman not a kovvn coun- cillor, or other public representacive. The " asso- ciation" have discovered they will be a power in the land ; they will be the " king-makera " of the "kingdom of Runcorn ;" t.ley will lord it over all, and dispense to all and sundry the seats npou the Council; and woe betide he who crosses their path. Such is the nature of the proclamation about to fall like a bolt frum the blue upon us townsfolk.

The work they have co face is said to be great. There is to be "fair frade " for the port of Runcorn, at dues similar to those of other ports upon the Ship Canal; concessories in railway freights; re- ductions in bridge fares between Runcorn and Widnes; electric trams and lighting, with recrea- tion grounds thrown in. All these things are to be taken in hand, and the Council instructed free in the art of municipal government. But we shall see what we shall see.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Wigan beaten easily by 24 points to nil, was the achievement of the ''Redtaile last Saturday. And every credit is due then too, for their play was that much superior. I don't go so far as to say Wigan played poorly; far from it they played a good game. But Runcorn beat them at every point, and showed more than ordinary ability.

It would be less than my duty were I to omit to mention the praise due to the referee who conducted the game. It was a pleasure to see football under his management; and were all referees to conscien- tiously discharge their duties as did "the man with the toot" at Runcorn, last Saturday, Northern Union Rugby would be a gentlemanly game.

February 10th takeg us to Salford, provided the ground will be fit. and I can promise Salford they will have to go all the way to stave off defeat if Runcorn get into anything like the stride they sometimes exhibited last Saturday. Of course there is a pmssibility of Runcorn going down,but no one in Runcorn expects a fall at New: Barns.

div.p: A CHILD DIES IN THE STREET.

At the Runcorn Poli,!a C-,urt on Monday. Mr. R Dob- PCM, coroner, held an inquest on the body of William Webb, five months old son of Either Webb, single woman, residing pith her mother at 4, Dutton's Court, Runcorn.—Esther Webb (the mother) having given evidence of identification ; said her child was barn on the 14th of August last. She noticed the child was 111 about 10-30 on t•unday, and took it straight to Dr. Robinson's. Be was not in. Sic was told to call again and did so Dr. Robinson then said the child was very ill, end told her t 3 go home with it. She left Dr. Robin- son's but found the child was dead in her arms when she had get part way home The child was always a healthy one, though it hid a clugh from its hirtb. would not take any food that morning.—Dr. J. B. De- laney said he had made Rpost mnrtem nxaminei -n of tlrt body.—The child appeared fairly well nourished .—From his examination he came to he conclusion that the chili died from bronchitis.—The jury returnad a verdict in accordance with the medical evidence.

Leonard Maddo3k, seaman, native of Runcorn, was on Tuesday apprehended by Constable Carring- ton, on a charge of stealing a pair of marine glasses frAm the ship "Allslrtross" lying at Liverpool, upon which boat he was lately employed. There was a good erten lance at this meeting on Sunday afternoon, when the chair was taken by the Secretary. The soloist, Mr. J Thompson, sang very effectively "Flow, ever flow," the chorus being taken as a quartette by Misses Hulme, Harrison, and Messrs. Thomas and Thompson. Mr. Thomp- son also sang another solo,which was well received. The President (Rev. J Pedlar) gave a short address on "Temptation." PLEASANT SATURDAY EVENINGS AT WIDNES. On Saturday evening last a large audience assem- bled at the Oakland-street Wesleyan Schoolroo m,th e occasion being the usual social meeting. Mr S Jack- son presided. The programme consisted of songs, duets recitations, and dialogues, and was ably carried out by the following :—The Misses Heather- ington, Woodward, and Ihrtland • Messrs W Shaw, F Littler, W Rogue, and the Oakland-street party. The items given by Miss Heatherington and Messrs W Shaw W tiague, and F Littler were productive of vociferous encores. The accompanist's duties were ably discharged by Mr W A Hague.—At the West Bank Mission a lantern entertainment was given, when the following subjects were illustrated: —" The Little Hero," "The Lifeboat,"" My First smoke," "The oiled feather," "The German musician in Africa," and " Sports in the Fiji Llands." An excellent programme of vocal and instrumental music,arranged by Messrs Gibbons and Wilson, was highly appreciated.

Shaw (missionary) and a few of his voluntary workers me:: at the Mersey Mission, on Tuesday eveni.ag, at the close of the usual weekly concert, and presented a Bible to Capfain and Mrs. Amsbury (of the " Puritain ") in rec3gnition of the valuable and kind assistance they had given to the Mission during their stay at Runcorn.—Captain Amsbury in accepting the present said on his own behalf and that of his wife, it was they who were indebted to Mr. Shaw and his co-workers for the admirable way in which they had enjoyed them- selves whilst in Runcorn.—The small assembly then sang" For he's a jolly good fellow,"" Auld Lang Syne," and" God save the Queen," after which they dispersed.

div.p: iICCIDENT AT THE DRILL HALT..

_ At the Drill Hall, Runcorn, on Wednesday night a serious accident occurred to Joseph Taylor, aged 11 years, ot" Okell-street. The youth was hanging by the rings of the Volunteer Gymnasium. A num- ber of companions were swinging. when from some cause he relaxed his hold and fr.ll to the floor alighting on his head. He was picked up in an un- conscious state and Mr C J Allen, electrical enjneer of the Manure Works, Old Q lay, rendered first aid in a manner that won him the appreciative thanks of Dr. McKenzie on his arrival. The boy was carried home and remained unconscious through- out the night suffering trom severe concussion ot tie brain, and probably other injuries. MA.URIAGR OF A RUNCORN FOOTBILLER. •

On Tuesday afternoon an interesting marriage took place in Runcorn Parish Church in the presence of a large congregation. The bridegroom was Mr. Samuel Walker, Runc9rn Football Club's celebrated forward, who has played for the County of Cheshire for nearly ten years, and his union to Miss Annie Shaw was witnessed by large numbers of his club mates. Miss Sarah Walker was brhiesmaid and the cereormy was performed by the Rev II B Firth. The happy couple received the congratulations and gooil wishes of many friends and the presents were both handsome and numerous.

div.head: VOLUNTEER' SATURDAY NIGHT CONCERT
div.p: VOLUNTEER' SATURDAY NIGHT CONCERT

Another capital entertainment was provided by the Runcorn Volunteer Corps, at the Drill Hall, Runcorn, last Saturday night. Captain George F. Aaron pre- sided, over an over-crowded attendance. The band opened the programme with "The Absent Minded B-ggar." Professor J. L. Wyman followed wi'h some "sleight of hand," tricks which were well received. Mr W. H. Ireland contributed "Mary "and wan encored. He responded with "Flight of Ages." Both pieces were well sung. The war in the Transvaal was then described with illustrated lantern slides. Miss E'hel Saunders re- cised the" Absent Minded Bee,gar " with eff ict, and a good collection resulted. Later in the evening so also gave the" Handy-man" and was loudly applauded. The band again figured at the opening of the second partiand contributed "The songs of England" introducing "Home Sweet Home." Mr Outhwaite wielded the baton with his usual effect. " Alice where art thou" from the lips of Mr Ireland was vociferously reeeived. Professor J. L. VVyman's exhibition of shadowgraphy which fol- lowed was the item of the evening, and created no end of amusement. The projectoscope showing new animated pictures, included " Krueer going 1,, the Vo ks.aad." "The attack on the armoured trai.,," and "Nurses attending the wounded," and did much to in- tensify the patriotic feeling of the gatheriag.—During the interval Captain Ashton took the opportunity of thankng Professor Wyman. Mr W H Ireland, Mr W H Ainsworth (accompanist), Miss Ethel Saunders and Mr Temperley, for the services they bad rendered during the evening. He also spoke with satisfaction of the way in which recruits were coming forward to j'in the ranks of the Runcorn Volunteers, being at least 200 per cent better than on any provioes occasion he could remember. The proceedings concluded with the National Anthem. The proceeds as usual go to the frwll find; for the relief of soldiers' wives, etc.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

. The monthly meetiu; of this Board was held at the Town Hall on Thursrlay evening, when th4.ro were pre- sent the Rev. Canon Mti,land Wold (chtieman), dr E Imison (vice-chairman), the Rev J Chambers, Mesirs James Pritchird, W J Cunt ingham, G W Lightburn (clerk), and A Lif.Yhthurn (assistant clerk).
IRREGULAR ATTENDANCE GREAT LOSS IN GRANT.

The Clerk sebmitted the report of the School Attend- ance Comtnittee for the year ending 29th September, 1899 The average number on school registera was 3,362, decrease (coeepered with previous year), 2; average attendance. 2,855, inerea-e, 11; percentage of attendances 849, incr as" 4 ; warning notices served by visitors 4,292, in-rase 148 ; parents before committee 755, decrease 19; prosecutions before magistrates 136,in• crease 63. The Clark had prepared a new table showing the number on regis'ers, average and percentages of each school in the town. The percentages were as fol- lows :—Victoria-road boy', 912 ; National boys', 894 ; Victoria-road girls', 83 6 ; National girls'. 835 ; Trinity Church mixed, 87 2; S. Blwards (R.O ) mixed, 79 4 ; Mill-brow infants'. 81 ; National infanta'. 84 7; Trinity Chureh infants'. 831 ; Granyille-strelt infants' 80 ; St. Elwarde's (R C.) infents', 77 5 ; Newtown infants', 80. The number of children of school age who had left the town during the year was 254. The number of Canal boat children was 101. The general report was as follows :—"lt will be observel that the attendance of infants is better and has nearer approached the level of that of the boys and girls, where the three departments (boles, girls, and infants) are taught in One building, due no doubt to the fact that the elder children of a family bring with them the younger ones to school. The number of canal boats registered in Runcorn is greater than at any p'ace in the United Kingdom, and if the attendances of beat children were exctuded from the calculations the percentage of attendance world be two per cent greater than now re- port,d, The percentage of attendances during the year ending 30th September. 1898, was the highest recorded, and it will be noted with pleasure the wecegtage of at- tendances this year exceeds that of 1898 Conspared with the whole country this remit is satisfactory, but com- pared with what might and ought to be it is depressing when it is considered that en every occasion the schools were open during the year an the average 507 children were absent. Children away on boats, those kept at home in consequence of sickness and other excusable causes, account for 134, leaving 373 cases of avoidable absence. These absentees form a class by themselves, and are for the most part the product of parental nezieer, land they are Fret the children who require most the moral restraint of a school. From a financial prid to nt of view the loss to School Board (ratepayers) ao the managers of the other elementary scheols in the town during the past year on these 373 children amounts to about £560." The Chairman said he was convinced that every member of this Board would feel that it was desirable to see not only that the child had Pow, -educetiog, but that that education should be as eoed as it possibly coul i be. The whole of the pa.ements, of whatever kind, from grants, grant on examination, or whether they were from attend ince fees, ware made in, one beeis, viz., that of average attendance. The consequence was that the loss of one child in average attendance probably meant a loss of 304 to the particular school to whi dr they be- formed. The matter had been put in a very remise and concrete form in the lost paragraph of the Clerk's re- port. It was there represented that there were 373 children habilmelly absent from school in the town, which meant a loss of £560 a year. He thought the parents and friends ef the children and the ratepayers as well ought to do really all they could by persuasion to vet the children to school, if thy were to consider that this £560 a year, which would mean something like 33. in the Z. was neeitiv,ly thrown away through a number of careless and irregular children wile ought to be at school. The Clerk explained that in arriving at the 373 children as trainer habituellv absent lee had allowed fer the boat children and also cases of sickness. The 373 Cases were clearly inexcusable. He had also been very careful in estimating the loss, and had not exaggerated matters. .

_ Mr Imison said he would emehasTza what the Chair- man had already said. In future, improvement in the average attendance could only bo the result of greater interest on the part of parents. They had almost exhansted the compulsory powers of the Board, and also the efforts of the teachers. They had recognized that the prevent attendance was eecur,d by the teachers, and school attendance officers, and they had reached the limit of their rowers. If they coill secure a greater in- terest on the part of parents. and a more real doire for the education of their children, then he thoueht they vreuld see a far greater improvement in the attendance than they were _ likely to see from any further nressure on the part of the Beard or its officers. (Hear, hear.) Mr Pritchard thoueht there veers nth"r features in the report which were Fatieractory. With regard to the question nf improvement in the attendance, they had been working at it now for a vartrr of a century. Ha thought they had made considerable ',regress in that time, and it would b.* the work of the Attendance Committee to Res it continued in the future. The report was adopted.

TWO MEN IN A BOAT. An Amusing Episode at Runcorn. I have often thought that the boy who was "taken up "for picking sticks on a Sunday was a hardly used little individual. Now Mark Twin's bad boy had a right royal time of it. Everything he touched turned up trumps as it were. His larks and escapades always turned out to his advantage, and the sorrowful ending of the Sunday School book stories was entirely absent. But Nemesis overtakes those who break the Sabbath in the long run. How often do we hear that if "So and So" had attended at Church or Chapel such and such a thing would not have happened. So would I say to the heroes of the short story I am about, to tell. Two gentlemen, each of the locality described in Runcorn as" Windy" and well known in their various avolations in life, went for a stroll on Sun- day morning in order to while away the time and prepare an appetite for the hot joint of their matu- tinal meal. Now this was no new venture, but on this occasion their fancy took a bolder flight. Ob- serving a boat on the pellucid waters of the Weaver canal, they determined there and then upon a voy- age. The man learned in finance took a seat in the stern and his more bulky companion, known to his intimates as "the millionaire" essayed to follow his example. One foot on shore and one foot on the boat he stood, in the attitude of a "Collosus of Rhodes," but his dignity was short lived, for when he attempted to lightly spring aboard he pushed the craft away, and took a header into the canal between the wall and the beat. Alarmed as he was the occupant of the boat seized the situation and a portion of the anatomy of his friend at the same time —and after great exertions drew him on board. Seconds sufficed to 7get th.rn to terra firma and quicker than ever before in their lives they sprinted up the hills of Weston, home, where a warm bath and a drop of the " Crater " put the shivering one all right, and his friends rejoice that he is once more himself and able to add this to the many personal adventures he has retailed for their benefit many times and oft. Of course this tale is unvarnished; the hero will supply the necessary polish when he personally recounts it.
SUDDRN DEATH AT RUNCORN.

Mr. R. Dobson, c3rnner, held an inquest at the Run- corn Pollee Conn on Mulch!, upon the body of Patrick McLean, of 5, Fryer-street, Runcorn; who died suddenly on Sunday morning last.—Margaret McLean, wife of the decees.d, gave evidence of identification, and described her husband as a rope-spinner. For some considerable time he complained of suffering from the "stuff " that he worked with, and also complained of pain. She th,ught it was bronchitis that deceased suffsred from. 01 the Saturday night he bad some gruel with a little whiskey in. She eot up on Sunday about 8 o'clock, aud left her husband in bfd. She took him the remainder of the whisky made up as punch ; and later called to him to enquire whether he would like anything else. She got no reply, and diecovered her husband dead.— Dr. J. B. Delaney was called in for the first time on Sun- day. Ho di;olyere.4 deceased had just passed away. From the history of the case, and the superficial examina- tion he made, it was his ooinion that deceased died from acute pneismonia.—The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical tostirnony.
