div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT'AT THE WHITE LEAD WORKS.
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT'AT THE WHITE LEAD WORKS.
Inquest and Verdict.

Henry Kendrick: 40 velr3 of age,eugitirer of 19; We!!.. fieid-street, died in the Infirmary at 745 on Sunday morning from effects of iLjeries receired whilst follow— ing his emnioynient at the Merge Wh:te Lead Works on January 19-b. It appears that at eleven o'clock on the date ir question deceaaed was engaged in putting a belt on the pulley wl;ic. eltives a fan. He was on a ladder about ten feet from the grouid, and gave the engine driver the sigral to start the engine. The driver (IA se and when he looked up shortly afterwards he saw the deceased going round the ehaft. He at once stopped the engine and the deceased fell on the vat below. Dr. Fos was called in, and ordered the deceas,d's removal to the, Infirmary, where he remained up to the time of his death.

Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, conducted the irquest a tht Plice Court on Tatsday. Mr. George Thomson, the mina: or. appe,:red on behalf of the firm, ad Mr. Smith, H.M. lop.peotor of Workshops and Factories was a!so present. Mr. D. Fanskaw attended on behalf of the relatives of the thaeased. Aagelina Kendrick said decease was her hasbacd. She saw him on he morning of the 19th ult. before he went to work. She he Ard of the accident about noon, and saw her husband at the Infirmary. She was with him almost the whole time unlil his d ,sth. He told her that the accident had occurred throngh a stud catching his slop. He was too ill to givo her any further _dhails, _ _

Mr. Fanshaw said he a ska-d deceased how the accident occurred. and 11,., said he was putting on a beltl and the stud in the shift cau.ght his slop. The Coroner ; Was the shaft revolving? Mr. Fanshaw said he nedereteod that the engine was stopped in the proper manner, and the foreman started it so that the deceased might put on the belt. That was usually done. James Huxley, foreman engiaeer, deceased's foreman said deceased had been employed at the works fifteen months. On the morning of the 19th deneasei told him to stop fh engine. The tan belt was then off. He did so, and deceased took a ladder and asconled it to put on the belt. When he had put it round as far as he could, witness started tho engine slowly, and the belt adjusted itself. He then put on a little more steam,lnd on looking up saw deceased on the shaft. He shut off steam very sharply. 'lite engine had gone round about twice. De- ceased had nut the belt on hundreds of times. The collar, which proj•,cte.l, must have c iught his clothing. The Coroner : Was the deceased to blame or was it the fact that the Icneb was proj-c:ing Witness: I earanot say. Mr. Thompson sail the arrangement of the machinery had been altered. Witness, continuing, said that when the engine was stopped the deceased fell on the vat, ten feet below. He was immi.diat ily taken to the Infirmary. The Inspector said he had v Fited the works, and had drawn the attention of the management to the projecting set-,crew on the shale collar. 111. should lik3 to pmpliasiz the danger of allowing prejections to exist in any revolving piece of machinery. Tnis was the second inquest he hal attended in the last five dacs where the accideat w,s shown to have resulte I from a projection 'in the machinery. These small things w, re responsible for a large number of accidents. It was a dangerous I and in a sense an illegal practice to approach a revolving shaft white in motion. It it were A -cessary, the shaft should to encased. 0.. e firm he knew, the management of which were impressed with the deair thility of making everything safe, had decided to have twelve miles of shaftimg encased to Pi event the possibilty of an accident. 13-At poles were used at :ioroa places to pet, on the belts, anl they were ale cited wherever possible.

The Jury returned a verdici of " Accidental death and recommeaded the carrying out of the Inspector's sureestion. The Coroner said it was only fair to state on behalf of the firm they had decided to have a fllnze pulley placed on the mach;nery. and he unclerstcod that that would pri,v,nt RC Mr. Fan-haw, on behalf of the f mily, thanked Mr. Thompson for his kindness to the deceased. Ht. had been most attentive and had extended every help that waS possible.

Information was given to the police, with a description of the girl who had been to the house hawking cakes. She was arrested near .z.he Central &Jahn' by himself and. Detective Forster and was then wearing the watch and chain. She admitted having stolen it and ;tido admitted hawing stoleu the articles named in the other charges.—The magis- trates' Clerk (Mr. G. F. div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
warrngton Borough Court.
FRIDAY. —Before the Mayor (In the chair), Councilloi Suzethurl. Dr. Gornall and Mr. tiepherd. _ _

Emma= or FAMILT.—Robert Samuel Poole. 21. Warbur- ton-street, was charged with having on the Bth of January and oth-r dates neglected his four children, Emily, Mary, Alice and Margaret in a manner likely to cause them un- necessary. suffering and injury to health.—He pleaded guilty. —Mr Browne prosecuted On behalf of the P.O 0. He said that that was practically a case where a man would do nothing but drink. inspector Hackett's attention was called to the man's family on Monday last, and he visited the house. He found the house was exceedingly clean and the children were clean, but very poorly clad. There was no bed whatever in the house. The defendant was a wire worker and could earn 33.3 a week, but he had not given his wife more than 5s per week for the last four months. The children had had to go out begging and a sister of the defendant and neighbours bad assisted the wife Inspector Hackett left word for the defendant to call to see him, and be did so the following day and promised to make amends. The Inspe3tor thought he was really going to imprcve as next morning the man went to his work at six o'clock. On visiting the 'lime on Tuesday night, the In- spector however, found the wife and children in the closet, the detendant havink turned them out of the house On going in the house he found the defendant lying in a beastly state of drunkenness across the hearthstone. The defendant would not work and his wife had to pawn almost everything In the house to buy food.—Defendant expressed his sorrow at what had occurred and said ha would sign the pledge if the Bench would give him a chance.—The case was adjourned tor a month to give defendant an opportunity of improving. Hollins Gr,ien, applied for cer- tain Indentures to be cancelled. He stated that a lad named Alfred fireball was apprenticed to him in January 1898, and he had to serve live years. The lad, however. ran away shortly' after ha was engaged, but returned, and had now run away again. In these circumstances he abked for the indentures to be cancelled. He had ascertaine 1 'hat the lad bad been apprenticed by the Board ef Guardians He did not know where he was now, but he understood that he had tried to get on board a ship at Liverpool. —The Chair- man : Why dO you want the indentures cancelled ? —Apoli- cant : Because he has run away —The Chairman: Is that the only reason ?—The applicant replied that it was. Shortly before the lad left he discovered a fire in his belroom. and it was extinguished with the assistance ot a neighbour. The lad then said he wanted to leave, and witness remarked it was strange he should want to go in the circumstances fir- eball then asked if he (the applicant) had set the bedroom on , fire, and the reply was " I don't judge you, but it is very strange."-- ihe Chairman said the Bench had decided to cancel the indentures. Wesleyan Infant School, Sankey Bridges. The intantg at the Wesleyan day school, trinkey Bridges. provided a pleasant evening's entertain- ment in the schoolroom on Friday and again on Saturday of last week. On both ocea-ions there were large audiences. The infants school is a com- paratively new institution in the district, but there are now over 200 children receiving instruction, and solid progress is being made, The children per- formed their several parts in the entertainment in a manner which reflected the greatest credit upon lthe schoolmistress, Miss Wiloashurst, and her aegis- ! Vint, Miss Morrell, who must have bestowed much I time and labour in initiating the youngsters into their several parts. A number of the items had a military air about them, notably the gun drill, the war alphabet and the popular song "Soldiers of the Queen. The little dots entered into the spirit of the pieces and the result was a very successful per- formance. Mr. Walter Brough presided, and com- plimented the teachers and scholars upon their work. The proceeds were in aid of the school funds.

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 9, 1900.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 9, 1900.
DEATH OF • COUNCILLOR JOSEPH
WILKINSON.

Yet another useful citiz-m of Warringt on has passed away in the person of Councillor Joseph Wilkin- sion, whose death took place at his reisidence, 60, longford-street, at 10.45 on Thursday last we7k. The decisased,asho was 71 years of age, had a stroke of paralysis in March,lB99,but he ral&d somewhat,and was able to drive and occasionally to walk about. About a month ago, however, he had again to take to his bed, owing to an attack. of bronchitis and dropsy, from which he never recovered, having only survived his wife seven mantis. He had been attended by Dr. For. lie was conscious up to the last, and his two sons, Messrs. John and Joseph Wilkinson, and his daughters, were present when he passes peacefully away. •Mr. Wilkinson was a consistent Liberal, and up to the time of his death represented Orford Ward in the Council. He had been a member of the Town Council continuously. since 1892. and was a member of tha Health, Sanitary Works, School At tendance, Cemetery, and General Purposes Com mittees— Mr Wilkinson was born in Warrington namely in Aketree-court, which is no longer in ex istence, and he and his family have always been associated with the fustian cutting trade. lie had been in business himself for half-a-century, retiring several years ago from any active part in his business, which was taken over by his sons under the title of John and Joseph Wilkinson. In 1897, they amalgamated with Jo.hn Platt and Sou,and the firm which is now known as Platt, .WilkinSon, and Company, employ a large number of hands. The deceased was a director of the company. He was a member of the Church of England, and was grailly resPeeted by all with whom he came into contact, and his death will be deeply regretted.

The grave closed over the remains et the late Councillor Joseph Wilkinson on Monday afternoon when all that remained mortal was interred at toe Warrington Cemetery with every mark of respect. A snowstorm swept over the burial ground during theinterment and this no doubt interfered somewhat with the attendance of the general public. There was, however, a representative attendance of the members of the Corporation of which the deceased was a member.—Tne funeral was attended by the Mayor (Alderman Roberts) and members and officials of the Corporation. They assembled at the Town Hall at half-past one in the afternoon, and drove to the late retodence of the deceased in Long- ford-street, where the funeral cartage was fermaii. At the head walked Chief Inspeztor Phillips,. Inspector Taylor, and a posse of police. They were followed by the carriages , containing the Mayor. Alderman Hutchinson, Councillors Bennett, Smethurst, Tinnion, F R Roberts, John Evans, John Baird, James Evans, F %V Monks, W Rogers. A J Jolley, L Greening; L llhlison, G Plomp. ton, A Peacock, and J Lee; Mr J Lyon WHittle (town clerk), Mr 'r Longdin (oorough surveyor), Mr GF F White (deputy magistrates' clerk), Mr F Taylor (secretary gas works), Mr W S Haddock (gas engineer) Mr R Norman (sanitary inspector), Mr John Clayton (Liberal agent), nod Dr Fox. Following the hearse were carriages containing the chief mourners, as fol- lows :—First carriage Mr John Wilkinson, Mr Joseph Wilkinson, Miss Wilkinson, Miss Annie Wilkinson and Miss Polly Wilkinson; second Master Joe Wilkinson, Mr John Crank, Mr Tom Crank, Mr Fred Savage; third. Mr Joseph Hewitt, Mr Ernest Hewitt, Mr Tom Knight and Mr John Knight; fourth. Mr Robert Hart, 'dr George Traviss, Mr Robert snd Mr W Fidler; fifth, Mr Henry Cochrane (Blackpool), Mr T Mather, Mr Smethurst. Mr John Griffiths; sixth, Mr Torn Connor, Mr Fred, Bonnell, Mr Bainea, Mr Mason (repre- senting Messrs Platt, Wilkinson and Co,) ; seventh, Mr Sheldon, Mr William Bar:oo,Mr Walter gannet', and Mr Samuel Floyd; eighth, Mr Peter Broadhurst and .Mr James Rush worth. At the Cemetery were Mr J II Hill, Hr W Rob.rts, Mr W Walker, Mr Jack- son Holmes, and Mr J Jeffrey,who,with Mr Clayton. represented the Liberal Club; and Messrs. Newton Wakefield, and J Taylor. The funeral service was conducted , by the Rev J Davies, vicar of St. Ann's. The coffin.which was of tlack fumed oak with heavy brass mountings, bore the inscription : —"ln loving memory of Joseph Wilkinson, died February 2nd. 1900, aged 71 years." Floral tributes were sent by Miss Wilkinson, Mr and Mrs John Wilkinson, Mr and Mrs Joseph Wilkinson, Mrs Crank and family, Mrs Hewitt, Mr and Mrs Savage, Mr and Mrs Boone)), Mr and Mrs Sheldon, Mr and Mrs Griffiths, Mr and Mrs Wake- field, Liberal Association, Mr and Mrs Rushworth, Mrs Woletencroft, Mrs Broadhurst, employees (two), Mr and Mrs Heaton.—The funeral arrange- ments were satisfactorily carried out by Messrs. W Mounfield and Sons.

div.head: ASHDOWN BALLAD
div.p: THE ASHDOWN BALLAD
CONCERT.

The concert- given in the Parr Ilaa on Thursday 14SG, uoler the direoa t'3l. is;r4.ld vu Ain - down Limited, the London music publishers, proved,from a musical standpoint, very di:appoint- ing. None of the vocalists evidenced consoicuous ability. Indeed it must be confessed that much of the singing was of a mediocre character. in fairness however, it is due to say that much of tne coldness and lack of enthusiasm shown by the fairly large 'company which had assembled to listen to the con- cert must be ascribed to its keen discrimination in regard to much of that "new music" which we understand it is theaobject of the concert-pßrty to submit to the public. While therefore we must express complete cmcurreace with the popular judgment which virtually pronounced many of the songs as wanting in interest or other raison d'etre, SOMA measure of sympathy must be felt for the various vocalists in the thankless task allotted to them. In one or two instances, when opportunity was taken advan- tage of to interpolate what may be described as one of the standard songs of the day, something much nearer succe,s was arrived at. But there was, irt the case of the tenor and the contralto at least, a deeper-seated reason for comparative failure in interpretation. Neither of th ase singers seemed to realise the artistic necessity of veiling bald transi- tions amongst the different registers of the voice which so often jarred upon the ear. The piano soloist played some compositions of his own and 5183 come well-known items, chiefly of a cantabile character, in a manner which gave unmistakeable evidence of good executive ability end taste. But it is unfortunate that he should not be aware how much his curious mannerisms at the keyboard dis- tracted ~;he attention of the listener. The violoncello solos were probably the most interesting feature of the evening's programme, and, save for a some what exaggerated rendering of the more involved passages of some of them, these may be fairly credited to the instrumentalist as showing distinct promise of ability when maturer years shall have more fully developed his powers.

div.head: ST. PETER'S CHURCH.
div.p: ST. PETER'S CHURCH.
Annual Tea Meeting.

The annual tea meeting in connection with S. Peter's Church, which WAS held in the sclools, John-street on Mondav evening, was attended with gratifying A•ccisS. The enjoyment. nowever, warsomewhat marred by the absence of theNicar (Rev. B. Percival), and the Rev. W. Bracenamp (curate), both of whom are coffering from a sevsre illness. At the rrquest of the Vicar. Ceuncilir John Roberts, acted ac chairman. At 630 over 2001 parishioners and friend partook of a capita tea, lady members oi the congregation assisting tt the tables. After tea, the room was c:e.red, and the usual ent-rtainment was held Daring the cauree of his introductory rernarirs, the Chairman ea-messed his deep regret at the abseece of their Vicar. Let them hope and trust , that he would have a speedy re- covery. It was Also very unfortunate that their Curate was suffering from a severe illness, wh7ch no doubt, to some extent, had been canard by over work They all blt very sorry for him and prayed that he and the Vicar would Imve a speedy recovery to enable them to continue their work in the parish. In conclusion Councillor Roberts announced that tar some tma they had been trying to get a new organ and in a few weeks they expected to have a most beautiful organ in the church. (Applause) The pro- gramme was then proceeded with. The first itctrn was a setection by the Wycliffe Band under the conductr,rhip of Mr W Brown, w ich was cralitably rPtVered. Mr L Aukiand was beard te advantage in" TLe Bug!er " and "The Old Brigade," and *IN Bate was cor.iiifly 'applauded for her interpretation of" A do!ly and a o Ach." A popular item was the " cake-walk "by the Misies Arline Harrison and Cicey Houghton, who ware vigorously encored. Later in the evening they gave a skirt dance which was equally well revived. Master J. Taylor contributed a violin solo" La Serentta " and Mr. H M. Ashton amused the aulience with a re,djug from Arternus Ward • rue humorist as Mr. A Grounds wivis, contributions created roars of laughter. Far hie " The Viller Concert "he was rrclled. Mr. F Webster ably accompanied. A vote of tie Aks wai ac- corded to all srlso had as4st din making the gatly-ring; a success and the prnceldings terminated with the singing of the Nstional Anthem.

div.p: WARRINGTON SUIRPRiSE BROUGHTON
RANGERS. The Backs in Form.

W4rrington played their return match with Broughton Rangers on datisrday at Whew:meg Field, and succeeded in defeating the homesters by 13 points to 10 after a verF goo:I game. " Smseic " Bats resumed his cap Wile; of the Warrington team after being absent since Chrktni as, and the team w as strong ali roand. Brough- toil were ful:y reprasextei, though Jackson was unable to perau4de the military authorities to allow him to playond Winakill officiated on the kft vying in his stead. Time was an atteadance of abut 4,003 spectators, and th ) ground was in very fair condition. During the first half of the game there was a slight fall of snow, but the vreath'r was in other reapacts favourable to the game. Mr. J. E. Smi:la (Widnes) refereed, and the teams in his ctiarge were compose.) as follows : W arrinaton : Hallam, full back : Fish, Isherwood, Smith i Jo:te?, three-quarters; J T Bate and Burgess half hacks 'aylor, Boardman, Morrisom, Scholtze, Antrobus, Wrevveather, Eden and Swift forwards, Broughton Rangers: W James, full back; Winskill, Barratt, Harry, and Lewis, three-quarters ; Nelson and Jame], half los-k1 ; Thompson, Whiteaead, Robinson, sjekawy, Eltrdisty, Welfenden, and Dsakin, f,:rwards.

Beta had his usual luck with the toss, and took ad- ireataga of a liaht breoze for the openiag moiety, Stick. nay 'setting the ball in motion. Feeble punting by both Flidcs followed, Fish finally gaining ground for Warring- ton, who attaakei. Hallam was tackled in possession, but the lianeara gained little. Jonee followed up a punt and in attampting to take the ball, knocked on. Everybady expectod the whistle to sound, but it did not do so and Burgess vary smartly snapped up the ball and raced over tha line. The Brdualatan people jeered derigivelir when Jones tried at goal, unsuccassrully. Haviag so fortunately got the lead, Warrington played a winning game. Toe backs put in a very pretty round of peasine, Fish making a disc along touch, only to be _ bundled into tae straw by Lewis. Broughton then colored the Warrington half by means of a fine forward rush. Ramat got away and threw .to Winskill, who made a powerful dash for the line, but Hallam brought him down finely. A smart tackle of the Rangers' cus- radian oy Fish gave Warrington the upper hand again, Burgess and Bite m akin headway by smart play. Isherwood received from Bate and running to Harry pagied neatly to Fish, and the two of them got throaeh the Broughton team by beautiful passing labor. wood grounding over the line, juet as the whistle blew for a doubtful parts. It was bard luck. Antrobus was wart held a veer fr ern the line.whila from the next pack Janee cramble for the corner but failed to score by inches only. S. James sent the ball out to Hallam, who .dropped at goal and hit thee upright. Harry attempted to knack the bill dead as it fell, but missed and the Warringten full hack racism up dropped on the ball to the Rangers' chagrin. Jones kicked a goal. Broughton made a tamporary run into the tVarrinaton half, wnere Hallam caused at:mists, by b•ine heid on the liar. Bats cleverly got the ball away however, Smith and Isherwood taking up the at- tack once moce, Broughton had an advantage forward, ,and by another dashing dribble drove Warrington half the length of the field, Fish luckily saving on the line. Another long pa?s Was went to Winsa ill who, had a fair opening, but Jones pounced upon him promptly. Bur- Les isawaie rather premature at the scrimmage and being penalised W. James dropped a fins goal from' near nalf way. Warrington were soon beck in the borne half, ane Fsa tried at goal from a difficult angle, bis kick falling about a yard short of the bar Barratt was tackled on the line, and S nith triad hard to get over,but was unsuccesisfu,. Just before the interval Broughton made another attack. S. James being very near scoring. The Warrington defeuce prevailed, and at half-time the core stood :—Warrington, 1 goal, 2 trios (8 points) ; Broughton:Rangers, 1 goal (2 points). Jones restartf d with a lengthy punt, and Deakin was tackled wear touca in the home quarter. Bate got away and threw to Jones, who was held at the corner. Harry now want fell back for the Rangers. W. James corning into the centre. Barratt dropped at goal from a favourable position but failed badly. The Warrington forwards dribbled away, hut were checked by W. James, who went dowa pluckily. Play pro:landed in midfield where Bata secured, and running thraueh he beat Barran arid passed to latter wnod, who ran up and fed Fish, the wing man rounding Harry and Lewis and exiting a fine try. He also kicked a geal, bringing Warrineton's score up to 13 painta. The Ran• gars were not disheartened however, and by a smart piece of passing reached the Warrington line. S James dodging over cleverly. He failed badly at goal however. Burgess then came to the fore with a smart run Worn the scrimmage and quick passing saw Smith run over and dash behhed the posts, only to be recalled for a presumable forward pass. A moment later Eden charged Harry's kick down and scored a per- fectly fair try, fahich was also disallowed. Winskill finally carried play into the Warrington half by a strong ran. Hallam was slow to respond and being tackled on the line he lost the ball, Hardisty pounc- ing on it rind scoring easily near the posts. Nelsoa kicked a goal,and brought the Rangers to withia a try of WirTingtn. Determined efforts were now made on both sides, bat Warrington's superiority was mani- reel. Borzess and Bate got away beautifully, and the ski oper elsould have scored but was afraid to trust him- self for the Short run necessary. The final came with Warrington winning a good game by 2 goals, 3 tries (13 points) to 2 goals. 2 Wee (10 pointe). Runcorn v. Wigan. They were separated by thousands of miles but she heard of him and came to him. We who hear of Christ by the word of Gad are responsible to come to Him. div.head: --4•-. THE LATE DR. PRESTON.
div.p: --4•-. THE LATE DR. PRESTON.

On Saturday the remains of the late Dr. W. D. Preston (son of the Rev. De. Preston, late vicar of Holy Trinity, Runc.)rn), who died at his residence, Mornington-road, Upper Beizliton, after an Hitless of three days, were in- terred at Flaybrick-hiil Cemetery. Birkenhead, in the family vault of the late Mr. Benjamin Derbyshire. The &ceased gentleman had made a name for hinaself at Mosborough, near Sheffield, where he was highly est.,emed, and also by the leadine. medical men of Suf- field. Toe chief mourners were Rev. Dr. Preston, Vicar of Raskelfe Rev. B S D&rhishire (father-in-law), Mr F Derbyshire (uncle), Mr W L Darhyshire (brother- in-law), Revs Edward Blakeney and J Leer Biakeney, Sheffield (cousins), DiPssra Nlrmau Darbyslaire (cousin), W G Liet,e and John Sner mood (unces), Frank Scephen- son (brother-in-law), and Dr Crook, of Egrecaont. Tbe service was read by the Rev E Blak.nev, M.A, vicar of St. Anne's, Sheffield, assisted by the Rev J Eiwards, late of Runcorn. The following members of the family wished to be present, but were unable :—Sir Cecil Moen, Bart., Rev J Darbyshire, Rev Stanley Darbyshire, Messrs E Darbyshire, 4 Glev-r, and H llizeins (Liverpool). REFERENCE AT RUNCORN.

Oe Sunday morning. at Holy 'Trinity Church.Runcorn tho Vicar (Rev C R Kinick. M.A.), in the course of a sermon, based on Job, xis,. 2, said " Many in this parish to-day will he tKinking of tire great trial which it has uleased Almighty God to send upon the late Vicar, who, for so many years, minWered here. His only son has been taken from him in the very prime of manhood. We all feel this morning the most sincere sympathy with the bereaved ones, and pray that Divine consolation may be abundantly ministered to them." The preacher referred to the many young and promising lives now bAmg cut off in the carnage of tne battlefield abroad, and by fell disease at home, and impressed upon his congre,gatiGn Use fact that the present life, brief and uncertain though it be, was yet full of the mightiest and most lasting issues either for annd or for evil. The Dead March was played at the conclusion of the service. In the evening the prayers of the cloc,,regathu were asked on behalf of the bereaved relatives.

div.p: TEE EXAM IN EP, FRI )A Y, FEBRUARY 9 1900 EARLESTOWN & NEWTON NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT PRIMITIVE METHODIST LADIES' :SEWING SOO lETY COUNCIL. EARLESTOWN. On Wednesday evening a social gathering in con- nection with the above society, was held in the Primitive Methodist Schoolro4m. About 120 people were present to supper, which was serve ti at 8 o'clock by the ladies. After supper an entertain- ment was given by members of the choir, and con- sisted of songs, recitations, &c. The proceeds were in aid of the trust fug, THEFT OF BOOTS AT EARLESTOWN. At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wed- nesday, before Messrs S. R. Armitage (in the chair) and Joshua Balls Alice Maud Thompson was charged with stealing a pair of boots valued at 7s lid from V4e shop No. 17, Bridge-street, Eerlestown, the property of Messrs Freeman, Hardy and Willis on January 27th,—She pleaded guilty.—Sydney Ernmerson, the maneger for Messrs Freeman, Hardy and Willis,said that at four o'clock on the afternoon of the 27th ult., the defendant came into the shop. She bought a pair of boots and paid 4i 141 for them. After she had gone out, the beots mentioned in the charge were missed and in con- sequence of what a boy told him, witness sent an assistant after the defendant. She was taken back to the shop, but denied stealing the boots. Tne boot a however, were found under her shawl. He was instructed to say that the firm did not wish to press the case. Defendant was under the influence of drink at the time she committed the theft.—Defendant was bound over to come up lir judgment if called upon,and ordered to pay the costs.

The Hope of Earlestown Lodge meeting was hel I in the Co-operative 114, Wargrave road, on Mon- day, Bro. Cutler, C.T. Aesiding. After the opening services the finance committee reported the fin- ances of the Lodges to be in a very satisfactory condition with a good balance in hand. The Secretary reported a membership of 113 the in- terest in the meetings being well sustained. The S.J.T. Bro Newman reported the temple in good working order with a membership of 94, and teat five members had sat for the National C egapetitive Examination four of whom had passed, Mary Simms having passed in the third class in the senior divi- sion, and John W Woods and Sarah E Clarke in the first class in the second division. Alice Roberts passed in the second class ia second division. The reports were adopted, the election of representa- tives to District Lodge then took place, resulting as follows ;—Bro Wood, Bro G Clarke, E.T., Bro Bro Warburton, Bro J J Leatherbarrow, Sister Woods.—Bro's 0 Clarke, Woods, Warburton, and Dring. were appointed to act. on t...e Juvenile Executive Committee. The following were appoin- ted to arrange for the next night's programme. Sisters Woods, Owen, Thomqs, Williams and icholson ; Bros. Warburton, Woods and Leather- barrow.—Sisters Woods and Croft were appointed to act on the programme committee.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS. BULLER'S NEW MOVE. Heavy Fighting Across the
Tugela.
Boer Position Captured.
Spearmin'd Camp, MONDAY NIGHT.

Under the personal direet.Jll of General Buller at. at- tack upon the Boer posltion blocking the road to Lady- smith was begun this morning at seven o'clock by nearly the whale ot our batteries, 72 guns shelling the ridges where the enemy had their trenches and re-doubts Brakfontein and the low crests facing Potgieter's Drift.

The enemy suffered severely, and several hills were smoking like volcanoes from the effects ot the bombard- ment, by which stores and grass were set on fire. Whilst a third pontoon bridge was being constructed under fire near Skeit Drift the Eleventh Brigarie, under the ccmmand of Colonel Wynne, made a demonstration against Brakfontein Ridge, marching across the meadows with the support of seven batteries of

a rtillory. The enemy at eleven o'clock opened a h?avy cannon- ade of shrapn, I, c-immon shells, and " p)m-pom" bhells, chiefly horn Spion Kop, accompanied by a rattling taus- ke'ry fire. Our guns behaved admirably and were as cool a 3 if upon parade. The demons!ration having gained its oti!ct, the real attack upon the Boer left was deliv.red. At tour p.m. the Durham Light Infantry carried Vaalkrant z, the key of the lower ridges, while General Fii:elyard's brigade assailed the lofts KraLzklocif. The General and his troops are bivouacking upon the field ot battle. Our losses are trifling. A Position Carried at the Bayonet Point.

A " Times " c,,rrespondent, in a telegram dated Spearman's Camp, Wedresday, says :—Yesterday no advance was made. In the afternoon the enemy vigor- onsty attacked the northern end of General Lvttelton's lyyj-. and at first were successful, but reinforcements arriving the position was recarried at the point of the bayonet. Macdonald's Seizure of Koodoosberg.

div.head: Boers' Uusuccessful Attempt to Rush
div.p: Boers' Uusuccessful Attempt to Rush
the Position.

A I,:affan's telegram from Koodoosberg Drift, via., Modder River, dated February 6, 1.50 a.m., but delayed by the Censor, says that a strong force of mounted B:;ers attempted at noon yesterday to rush our position at Kopdoosberg. The attempt failed entirely, and the enemy did not even succeed in ascertaining the strength in which we held the position. Our Engineers stationed on the top of a hill heliog,raphed that eur northward Lancer pickets were retiring in our direction. Th Beers in sections filed over a low ridge about 5,000 yards north of our position and immediately extended on the veldt below. They numbered at this time abut 500 men. As they advanced towards us at a gallop we opened upoa them a sharp fire from rifles and two Maxim guns. They worn constantly reinforced until their numbers had increased to about 1,200. Most of them loft their horses in the shelter of dongas and skirm- ished persistently forward on foot towards our trenches. They failed, however, to move us and had themselves tl rAtire before the fire of our screened infantry parties and Mlxims. Another party of about fifty Boers appeared this morning. The lancers emptied three of their saddles.

div.head: Further Presentations to Runcorn Volunteers.
div.p: Further Presentations to Runcorn Volunteers.

On Sunday afternoon Private L. edacz visited the Camden Sunday School attired in his khaki unifsrm,and his appearance was the signal for a tremendous outburst of cheering. Private Mack has been connect, d with the Camden School for some years, and the teachers and scholars decided to mark their sense of his selection for active service by presenting him with a small volume of the knapsack bible, bound in khaki. The gift was handed to Mr Mack by one of the superintendents, and the recipient expressed his thanks in a few well-chosen remarks —An interesting presentation was made at the Parish Church Sunday Schools on Sunday afternoon. One of the members of Mr W. E. Dudley's bible classes, Private David Chadwick, who is going on active service, was presented with a hanchome portable writing case by the members of the class. The presentation was made by Mr. Dudley, who expressed the high regard in whichiPrivate Chadwick was held, and while they were sorry that he was to New them, yet they felt proud that one of the class had been chosen to assist in maintaining his country's honour. They wished him od•speed and a safe return.—Private Chadwick, in replying, said he was unable adequately to think them for their useful gift, and for their kind expressions. He recognised that it was a serious matter to leave a good home and situation, but he lilt it hie duty, in the hour of his nation's trial ,• to take up his rifle, and do his level beet to help in repelling her foes. He assured them that whatever might be his fortune, he should carry with him the pleasantest memories of the hours he had spent in the class, and when far away their gift would re- mind him of the esteem in which he was held by the members.

div.head: Runcorn Soldier's Unpleasant Experiences.
div.p: A Runcorn Soldier's Unpleasant Experiences.
The followiag letter has been received from Private W. Spencer, Ist South Lancashire Bat' alinn. Thursday, 28h December, 1899.

Dear Uncle,—Just a few lines to let you know we are having a very bad time of it between the heat in the day time, and the rain at night. It is terrible. We can get nothing but water to drink, and it is not very good. We go out every morning at five looking for the Boars for about four hours. I had a splendid Christmas box. It was thundering and raining very heavy, and our tent was blown down about half-past twelve ; and we had to sit in our ehirts and we got wringing wet through. We had a big fight here the other day in which the Dublins lost 280 mfrn. It was a terrible alaughter. They dropned like stones going up the hill. It was all the fault of one of the officers. We have captured about 3,000 head of cattle and about nine spies. I had a terrible night last night. I was on out post duty, about three miles and a half from the camp. There were about fifteen of us. It is not a very nice j-,13 at night. I tell you thirteen men lie d .wn and two go out in front of them on sentry. They are all double sentries here, because one man could not stop by himself at night. You fancy all sorts of things. It rained all night, and we had to lie doe nin it with the result that we were sopping and very nearly perished. Just as it came day break, when I %, as on sentry, I thought we were poing to have a lively time before breakfast. I saw ahout a hundred of them (Boers) crming over a hill 'bout a mile away; hut they went back again and we not see them afterwards. There are 3,000 Boers cut off from the main body, and WP are waiting for them to come out, an 6 I made sure it was them. We re going up to the front very soon cow. Sir Charles Warren has come, sa no more at i re- ent, from y' ur nephew, BILL.

div.head: Another Letter from a Warrington
div.p: Another Letter from a Warrington
Police Constable.

P.C. Howard (29) has receiv, d the following letter from P.C. Hurst,now at the front:—"Saturday,Jan. 13'h 1900. 3341,J. HurA,4th Company 3rd Grenadier &lards, South African Field Force, South Africa. My dear old squad. chum,—Just a few lines to yrn,hoping my letter will find you quite well, and ali the bos teAdes. I am pleased to say that I am in the best of heakh. I Ell3ll be glad when all this is over, but we have a lot of work to 4o yet. We have had four battles already, and three 'intones, but the last time they were too many for us. Vid are now at Moddpr River, and shall be for a few %reeks until we get reinforcements ; then we will have another scrap,' and we live in hopes. of giving them another lot like we gave them at Belmont. They aid not
forget that for a while. It was a dreadful Mita to see. We charged them with the bayonet before they knew

div.head: Effects of a Shell.
div.p: The Effects of a Shell.

- The followine is a cepy of a letter weice his Won re- , ceived from Pdvate J. T. Gerrard (No. 8 Company 3rd Bettelien Grenadier Guereo) and is addressed te Mr.; Themes Gerrard, of 73, Fele-Ilea, Warr! ,gton. It is headed 'January 9.n, 1900, Welder River '':—" At ; present -we are staying at ilcideer River Camp. We don% know when we shall move. I have just come off ' outpost duty this morning. The Boers were firing at all y.!sterday, tout about thve o'cleck ono of cur !zune silenced them. A shell dropped amoug thirty of them and killed nine. For the last week we have been making a redoubt. It is a very big one. It is just is front of the Boer position.. They were firing on us all the time, and tiliy dropped a shell on the top of the trench and wounded two and killed one Cold- stream Guard. When we were on (outpost duty, we captured a prisoner who was sigualling to the Beers out of his house with Lights,so the Captain told me and thr, e more and a corporal to go to hi i hesie and cepture We crept round his house and got through the window and collared him and two more Necks. I hope you en- joyed your Christmas and New Year all right. I thouelet we should have been in Kimberley for Now Year's lay but we have another big battle to figh yet at Sypfontein —the place wh re we had the other one. We are 22 miles from ir.emberlev, and I hope and trust we shall all get safe there. So n more at present frem your loving seri JACK. P.S.—Give my le-:e to Harry end Clara and tell tle m I will be able to spin them some yarns when I come home, which I nape aed trust, in toe Lord I shall." Another Letter from Corporal J. W.

div.head: Dobson.
div.p: Dobson.

Corporal J W. Dotson (8810), 38th Company, A.S.C., Soucu Africa, writing to his roomer, Mrs. J. Dobson, Blackbear House, Knutsford-road, Warrington, under data January 8, says :—" lam pleased to ',dorm you teat lam ,rdt in the laud of the living and enjoying pretty good health. I have just arrived here (Stellen- bosch) from Molder River w /stria we have been havng it pr. tty stiff, I cao Issure you Night after nieht have we tried to sleep .eote the hire vo,nd for a boa, one's helmet for a pillow, and the sky above for a blanket ; and many a face have I s-en bright and fresh in the morning that has been cold and lifeless at night. This is a terrible war ! We are not only fiAlting the Boers but every nation on the face ef e tith, our own in eluded for amongst the prh,oners that have been taken- English, French, ant, German have been discovered. I thief: myselt that it will ,ake fully twelve months before it i seitted aed to explain the thing in one sc:., mean, the f Jlowieg, viz :—lt one man fastens himself in his own house, with plenty of everything be wants includ- ing firearms, etc., fancy the number of men he can kill before they kill him. That is just how it stands out hen only instead of houses they have hills full of recks and trees, etc., and as we take one posi'ion they simply move off to another, and perhaps all our trouble, independent of lose of life, has been for nothing. But what can we do ? They won't come out in the open (I—n fools if they did !) have all the best positions, and know every inch of the ground. What England requires now is that little word —Oprn sesame. I think I shall to stationed here for a few weeks and I am cot sorry as I look forward to hav- ing a line from you and forwarding yon a letter every week. My next letter will contain some curies,amens:st which will be three three-penny bits with old Kruger's mug ; and as no more of thtse will be issued they are priceless, I can tell you. I would like you to have them made inte some small ornament in memory of the battle of Graspan, for I found them concealed amongst seme bullets in a Boer's belt. Speaking of belts reminds me that the one I have got if it could speak, could say a god deal, as I always wear it. lam very sorry to inform you that one of the pr or boys who missed the 'Rapidan,' and who did not arrive here till eleven days after the vessel arrived has just been sentenced to 121 months' imprisonment, which, I suppose, would have ! been my fate had I not arrived here before her, But ! never mind, the Boers haven't copped Billy yet and I don't care a continental as long as I'm a colonial."
The Late Lieutenant M'Corquodale.

The" Liverpool Daily Post " says :—" We referred in this column some days ao to the deep regret felt in this neighbourhood at the death, at the battle of Spion Kop of Lieutenant H. Stuart M•Gorquodale, son of the late, Colonel WCorquodale, so weil kuown and popular in Lancashire. It appears toat the battle in which he fell was Lieutenant M‘Corquodale's first engagement. Be was with Thorneycroft.'s Horse, which took ellen a brilli- ant part in the four days' operations north of the Tugela. Lieutenant M'Corquodale was one or the unofficial special correspondents of the "Liverpool Daily Post," and like some of his fellow-officers, would no doubt have ren- dered us good service had he been spared. He only left this country in December, and immediately on hii ar.ival, with that high patriotic fervour which has characterised all classes in the war, volunteered for the front. He was a bright young fellow, with a fine military spirit, and had served five years in the volen- t.ers. Mr. M'Corquodale was unmarried and very great sympathy is felt for his mother and relatives."

div.head: Presentation to a Warrington Volunteer.
div.p: Presentation to a Warrington Volunteer.

A smoking concert Wd3 held the other evening at he Stag Inn, Lower Walton, for the purp-se ot making a presentation and wishing " God-speed" to Mr. Tom Massey of Lower Waito 1, one of the Warrington Volun- teers who has vo'unteered for servica in South Africa. The concert was attended by about fifty of his friends. The ctair was taken at 8 o'clock by Mr. El Hopkins. Songs were rendered by Messrs. Hatton, Woods. Davie, Bond, and many others, and the usual toasts were drunk with musical honours. Mr. Bond in making the presentation of a purse, which was subsc.ribed for by his friends, briefly spoke of the good feeling which existed among them. Mr. Tom Niassev responded, and a hearty vote of thanks was given to the Chairman,Mr. Bond, and the committee; also to Mrs. Maddock, the hostess. A very enjoyable evening was brought to a close by the singing of the National Anthem.
"Send off " at Workingmen's Mission.

On Monday evening. an enthusiastic "send-off" was given in the VVorkingmen's Mission Schoolroom (Tnewlis street) to Mr. John Charles Ilassall, a Warrington Volun- teer in the South Lancashire Regiment; and to Mr. Harry Baguley, a secor,d reservist of tha Ist South Lan- cashire Regiment (also a member of the St. John Ambu- lance Brigade). At 8 30, 80 of their friends sat down to an excellent tea, provided for the occasion by the Misses Birch, and other lady friends. After the repast had been partaken of, sp echcs were. given by Messrs. Nathan Hough, G Dale, r Duly, and T Ashley, who wished Ilassall and Baguley "GA-speed." Mr. T Ashley then presented both with a writing-case—a present which will no doubt prove useful ,during their forthcoming ex- pedition. '[hereupon Hassan and Baguley suitably responded by thanking the members present for their kind remembrances and good wishes. Ibis was followed by a short musical programmo. "The Soldiers of the Queen" was tastefully render, d by Mr. S Gough, and in respriase to an enthusiastic cnc,are he sang "The Boys of England." Mr. Sam Hassall's rendoring of "The Soldier's Toast" also called for an encore, to which be responded with "Let me like a soldier fall." The proceedings were brought to a close with the ainjrag of the National Anthem, in which all present heartily jo Red.

div.head: GILCHRIST LECTURE AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: GILCHRIST LECTURE AT EARLESTOWN.

The second lecture of the course was given in the Town Hall, Earleetown, on Monday evenine, before a_ large audience. The lecturer was Professor J. G. McKen chick, M.D.. L.L.D., ace., Professorpf Physiology in the University of Glasgow, and the subject " How we hear Musical tones." Mr. Arthur Sm,th presided and with very little preliminary introduced The Lecturer, who prefaced his remarks by a descrip- tion of the sense organs. We all knew, be eaid,that we got our information about the outer would by means of the sense organs which were attuned for the reception of different kinds of expressions. The impressions were conveyed by ware movements of which there were various kinds, come of whin we cool feel and see, such, as, for example the clouds, or the waves upon the surface of the sea, but there were other movements of a somewhat iernilar character which we could not follow. The phenomena of light and electricity depended upon wave movement. In these days we had all been startled by the investigation by another form of wave movement, wireless telegraphy, and there were movements of a more delicate character such as the movements of molecules. There were struc- tures in the internal ear which were adapted for picking up the waves of sound. In the skin for pickioe up special signs of touch, and in the nose for smell. Each organ was attuned for its particular kind of stimulus. Wave movement aff, cted a particular part of the sensory apparatus, and the nerve carritel the sensation to the brain. Sound outside our bodies was a physical move- ment and consisted of waves through the air inside the mechanism of the ear carried the sensation to the brain, and we had sound. There were various kinds of sounds which were described as noise, and others as musical soun2a. Noise very often may bs produced by the conflict of a number of musical tones. For instance, when they put the hand upon a number of keys of the piano, that produced noise. When they spoke of a pure musical tone, it was comparable to a sensation of pure light, as when they looked at a rainbow. The tones pro- duced by a musical instrument and the human voic were not pure tones, but mized tones. Tones could he blended together so as to preduce colour of tone, and the reason why one instrument was d fferent to an- other was that the tones were mixed tones. All musical tones were produced by movement and were similar to the swineine backwards and forwards of a pendulum. They would no doubt have noticed the undulation:l on the surface of still water, caused by a pebble being dropped in. The wave movement in con nection with water was an entirely different thine to wave movement in relation to sound. The charaeteristics of wave of sound were totally diff >rent from the char- acteristics of wave on the surface of water. The complex tones produced by musical instruments were complex tones which fell upon the oar. Pitch depended upon the number of waves which fell upon the ear in a given time. Illustrating with a tuning fork, he said, suppose that fork sent out 100 waves in a second of time, the drum head of the ear would be pushed out 100 Imes. Pitch depended really upon the prevture upon thii drum head produced by the waves of sound. No doubt they had great pleasnre in listening to a very rapid pianist. The movements of the fingers were very rapid that per- haps in the tenth of a second they might hear a sound, and in the next instant a different sound of pitch, and the ear picked up the difference in tone and pi ch. Quality of tone depended upon the kind of wave falling upon the ear. When they had two things, tunrd to precisely the same pitch, one would cause the other to vibrate. The ear could analyse sound directly. We could pick out the particular sounds with the greatest nicetvlfrorn the general mass of sound sent forth by an orchestra. Re then proceeded to deal with the phlnrgraph, which he said was not a toy, hut one of the most scientific instruments. The principal of it was that they could cause vibration of a glass disc to be recorded oe a wax cylinder. He gave an illus- tratien of the working of the phonograph, and trans- mitting the seund by means of wires from the inetru• merit on the platform to arother on the gallery. _
At the close a 'iota of thank,: wAs psq;?o, rl the Lecturer on the motion of Dr. Lltham, secontird by Mr D. Forrester.
A similar complirnrnt. was paid the Chairman el th motion of th', Lr'eturor.

div.head: TRH MAYOR AND THE BRNEFITS OF TM& CHAMBER
div.p: TRH MAYOR AND THE BRNEFITS OF TM& CHAMBER

Toe MAYOR, ia moving dee adeption of tne report which was published in " Tue Examiner last week, ernphasztd the fact that during the year the work of the chamber had beau quiet anu unostentatious. There were one or two matters mentioned in the report which were worthy or the consideration of commercial men and manutacture:s. la connection with the general utility of the chamber, he did net think it was suffi- ciently appreciarod that it could be made use of by busi- ness Inri to an extent which was calculated to he of considerable benefit. He had an instance in his mind when his own firm less tean 12 months ago were anxious to make some inquiries in regard Co a possible source of supply ot in ateriil• They utilized the chamber for that purpose* (he institutian, not because of its own strength, but because of its being one ot a large associated federation, lied a regard paid to any inquiry it made which would no be paid to individuals making inquiries on their own account. Through the British Consular Service they had oppertuuities of obtaiaing information that was both valuable and useful ; and in the panicular instaace to which he had referred his firm secured business to tee amount of ever £3o,ooo—a fact which was wot.th no';ing, and oegirt to be a soerCe if enceur-agemeat to other firms. Ha was afraid however, thet from want of appreciation of the pos4ibilities the chamber a 'forded people did not avail theinseeves of it. He stated the fact became he hoped it would lead to an acquisitien of members. (Hear, hear.; Alluding to the forthcoming industrial exhibitien at Parr Hall, the Mayor said he hoped the maaufac- Curers and mereeants and other business men would give it :hat supp 'rt it deserved, as the management this year would be in th hands of local man entirely. a', lived it would not fall short of the success which the two previous exhibi eons had attained. (Hear, hear.) Oa the errestion of the proposed technical insti- tute, the alderman said that for some time pest, the necessity had barer felt for making in ire ample provision for tee teaching of technical in- struction. That very important question was likely *e be put before the Corporation very shortly in a form which wou'd make the proposals worthy of very serious consideration. It was ouvious that every year increased the competition which the manufacturers of the United Kingdom had to contend with—ea competition which as tar as continental rnnufacturers were concerned was a c)mpotition pr ,duced by intelligent application of scien- tific and commercial knowledge to the various depart- ments of trale. It behoved them, if they were to maintain the positicn which this country had held for years, to see to it that their artisans were educated up to the highest point in referenee to everything which could be made applicable to the pursuit of their own particular line of trade. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Rime FAIRCLOUGH seconded the adoption of the report, and said the chamber was working in harmony with the various ckambers and any information which it 'might he difficult to get personally was obtained with ' the assistonce of the associated chambers.
Mr. FULTON SMITH said if the local railway companies would attend to their traffic hotter it would help the trale of th- town somewhat.

Mr. FAIRCLOUGH : There has been a great scarcity of wa2gons. Mr. Fuvrox SMITH said the firm Le represented had been hampered very much during the past nine months, and th,, railway companies never seemed to be prepared for a holiday. The MAYOR said he cou'd fully sympathise with what had been said about the shortness of the truck accpm- modation. It had been simply appalling tor nearly 12 months now, Mr. FULTON SMITH: It was not much better las wk.

The SECRETARY remarkrd that representations had been made to the London and North-Western Railway Company with tit fevnce to the inad quate train service, and they had received the usual official intimation that their letter had been received. They had heard nothing further yet. Mr.Fuvrox SMITH: It is a piece of red tapeistn. The MAYOR announced that the Corporation were asuisting in the representations with regard to the local railway servio ; and from what they had heard in- directly they believed their recommendation was likely to receive favourable consideration very quickly from the London " at,d North-Western Railway Company. (Hear, hear.) The motion was agreed to. ELECTION OV OFFICERS.

Kis Worship the Mayor was re-appointed president Mr. C. E. Parker, vice-president ; and the Mayor of Warrington f..r the time being, and the ea-Mayor, ex- officio members of the Council. Mr. W. Skinner (Parr's Btnk Limited) was appointed hon. treasurer, a vote of thanks being accorded to Mr John Murray for his pist services, and Messrs Ziba Armitage and Thomas Tun- stall hon. auditors. The hon. secretary is Councillor Bennett. Ail the officers were thanked for their ser- vices.
THE VALUE OF COMMERCIAL EDUCATION.

The SECRETARY read a letter which he had received from the Bradford Chamber of Commerce, the obj ct of which was to induce the Government to encourage the teaching of commercial subjects. Be had received another communication on the same question frown the London Chamber of Commirce, advocating a echeme of commercial ex tmination and suggesting a local centre for that purpose. The MAYOR Said they could support the proposal of the Bradford Chamber to recommend the Government to make grants in aid of commercial subjects as well as in science and art subjects. He moved that they present a mem.rial to that effect from the Warrington Chamber.
• Mr, FAIRCLOUGH seconded, and the motion was agreed to.
LOCAL TRADERS AND TEE SHIP CANAL.

The SECRETARY said they had had an exhaustive re- port on the subject of the lay-by at Stag Bridge from the Ship Canal Company, but it was extremely discour- aging. The authorities seemed to say that there was a want of co-operation amongst the Warrington rhanufan- torers, and that the lay-by was built under the impres- sion that it would receive greater support than had actually been the case. It seemed unfortunate that they should have a lay-by at their doors and not be able to make any use of it. The general body of the public up to now had received no benefit whatever, and if they could as a Chamber do anything to lead in a small way to the utilisation of the canal, they would be doing a public service. (Hear, hear ) The Corporation had power to construct a dock in Warrington during a cer- tain limited ime, but at present there was no earthly encouragement to do anything in that direction. Not the slightest preliminary preparation had been made for anythilg of the sort. Time was slipping by very rapidly and it seemed as if Warrington would be without a dock for all time. Perhaps the little interest taken in the matter was due to the commercial prosperity of the town. He felt that other towns with the same opportu- nities would have utiliaed the canal to a greater ex- tent.

The MAYOR observed that it was only fair to bear in mind that private enterprise had done a great deal on more adyantageous terms for the trade of Warrington than the facilities afforded by the lay-by, in connec'ion with the charges attached to the use of it, including tolls, would bring about. When they remembered the enormous volume of trade carried via the Ship Canal to the various works and wh-irves for manufacturers, mer- chants, and others—it would be seen that Warrington was taking a very appreciable amount of support from the canal itself. Because the lay-by was not used to the extent they would like to see itsit did not follow that the traders were standing still and making no use of the canal. On the c-eitrary, they were making a substantial use of it. The SECRETARY : But do not your remarks, Mr. Mayor, apply to those situated on the canal ? rho MAYOR: On. no._
Mr. FULTON SMITH: We have the drawback of send- ing goods to Manch ster and then bringing them back to Warrington. The use of the lay-by would obviate that.

--;i1;e1 MArott said all the trade that came to Warrington in bulk was prHctically being brought by water, but there were a number of traders of smaller calibre, shop- k,Tpers ad oth re, who received parcels whose trade in the aggregate w.s con,i(lerable. But it was not sufficient to any individual trader to induce a shipping company to stop their vessels at the lay-by. The result was that the vessel went right up to Manchester and discharged its cargo thcre, and what was intend 'cl for Warrington was barged back. Until there was some combination on the part of these small traders th,mselves to secure any ad vantage that mighl', he pois.blo by arranging that their materials should be brought up as one parcel, and getting them to stop at Walton, they could not do anything. The SECRETARY pointed to the desirability of combina- tion among the local traders interested. Unity was streneh. Acting alone they T:vould never get these f

The Late Mr, John Hartley. "The Warrington Grcuit Wesleyan Methodist Chace') Record"says rh, Kirg of errors is work- ing dreadfui havoc among the children of men jd now. The war in 'outh Africa closes the career of many a noble life, and is the prelude to many an aching !iefirt and falling tear. It seems as if the death knell were constantly tolling. We have had a sad experience at Latchford recently, and our church has lot cow of its prominent and most u,e- ful members by the death of the late Mr. John Hartley, of Sunnyside. Gloking hack, it seems but yesterday that we saw him occupying his accus- tomed seat in the sanctuary;but a change has taken plac-1, a sofa in our church has been vacated. But the pew is not the only place in our church where our fri,-kod will be missed. How frequaatly he stood at the doors to w,!leorrie people, for he thought it an honour to be a doorkeeper in the house of God. Probably none will miss him more ou:side his own home than the young men. He did much to add to their comfort,basides the kind words that fell from his lips at times which will linger with some of us- for many a day. Yea, perhaps, for ever, for "kind wor .s can never die." Would to God that each of us—when the closing scenes of this life admits us to eternity—may leave behind us such like impressions and hallowe.l memori.-s.

div.head: Death of Mr. John McDowell
div.p: Death of Mr. John McDowell

We regret, te k.aee to record the death of Mr. John McDowell, which took place at his residence, Re lands-street, at an early hour on Sunday morn- ing, at the ripe 01,-1 age of 81 years. The cause of death was bronchitis fell ;wing influenza. The deceased's medical attendants were Drs. SherratO and Langdale. Born in the north of Ireland, Of Scotch perentage, the deceased came to England in the year 1816, started business on his own account in 1850 in Liverpool, and removed to Warrington 10 1867, where he took over the whole business of Maskery and Co., with breneues at North wich and Liverpool. He practically retired from it about tem , years ago, and the business since then has been conducted by three of his sons under the title of McDowells, Limited,of which company the deceased gewleinan was citairman of the directors. He wile a man of great business capacity and indomitable energy, being also most methodical in his habits. He leaves a widow, five sons, and one daughter (who is the wife of the Rev Lewson Burnett, of Donaghenore, Count y Down, Ireland). Mr McDowell was a Conservative in polities, although he took no active part in them after leaving Liverpool. He attended St. John's Presbyterian Church, in win- wick-street, and was One of the elders of the Mall" chester Presbytery. The funeral took place at the Cemetery on Weeneeday afternoon at 2.30. Nursing Association.—Concert in Parr Hall. Parr Hell was weA filled on Saturday evening, when a concert, the procee,,s of which were in aid of the Warriugtou and District, Nursing Association was held. An excellent programme was submitted, several well known artistes taking part. The greater portion of 'he entertainment was supplied by Mr. T. J. Down's military baud, Mr. Down con- ducting with his usual ability. Their contributiofl! w-re, the selectioes : "The Princess o Trebizonde and "A Runaway Girl ;" march, " The Soldiers Of the Queen ;" valse, "Die Hydropaten ;" overture, "Crown Diamonds ;" and Mason's fantasia, " The Life of a Soldier,"eaeli item being received with loud and prolonged applause. Mr. Thornborough (tenor) was successful in his rendition of the patriotic song 'The Queen of the Sea" which elicited the warm ap- plause of the audience. He also sang" The Blows iv on the nye," and" Love's Request," with Equally good effect. " Happy youog Heart" and •' The Minstrel Boy" were almirebty sung by Miss 1%.1 Langdon (soprano). The humorous e:ement was Ist the capable hands of Mr Walter Wade, whose effortre to amuse met with the greatest success. Mr W f Payton accompanied. The proceedings were brought to a close, with the rendering of " Rule Britannia" and "God save the Queen," by the band.

NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. [By "Ovalist.":" Notwithstanding my disgust at recent performances by the Warrington team I ventured to predict a victory for them at Broughten. What made me do so I cannot ' quite say, except that I thought Warrington were really the better team, man for man. For a wonder they verified my prophecy and defeated the Rangers at Wheater's Field for the first time in the history of the Northern Union. The superiority of the wiriness was very marked, tboneh the final score was 13 points to 10, and did not give Warrington much of a margin. Even the Broughtonians admitted that the best team had won and in fact the Warrington men gave one of those dis- plays which one always expects from them, but seldom sees. There are hopes for the cep-ties oven yet. The game was a splendidly contested one right through.Warringten's superiority Watt solely in the back division and the excellence of tee Broughton forwards prevsnted play being at all one-sidfid. Early on a slice of luck, such as W:rrieeton seldom get, came their way. A palpable knock on by Jo lea was allowed to pass unnoticed by the referee, and that lively youth Burgess profited by the general dumbfoundedness to snap the ball up and score his first try for Warrington. Yells and execrations by the Brouebtonians had no effect on Mr. 3 H Smith, but they apparently spoiled Jones's goal- kick, for it was wide of the mark. "Nothing snceeeds like succ;ss " is a trite and true saying. Warrington made rings round the Brousbton backs after this and the patchier at times was warmly applauded. It was not very long before t'?e second score came, and oddly enough this W:l3 itetle.Jly luoky. Hallam to* a good opportunity to drop at goal, and hit the upright. The nail fell over the line, ark! Harry making a careless attempt to send it deal had the mortification of seeing Harem race up and score a well.merited though lucky try. This time Jones made no mistake with the goal kick. Some end tepid play followed, the borne front rank occasionally °ening all before them to the War- rington line. In one of these temporary incursions they obtained a penalty,W Janaes landing a good goal, so that the state of the game at half time was 8 points to 2 in Warrington's favour. Broughton had the wind in the second.half and were ' expected to do better,nut they gave no promise of doing so for long time. Bete and Burgess made some grand openings for the Warrington three-qnerters,whese move- ments were beautifully combined and always dangerous. From one of these Isherwood gave Fish a nice chance, and the active left winger was soon over the line, after- wards hacreasing the agony by kicking a cleverly-judged goal. Tee game now seemed over—bar shouting—but the Rangers" bucked-up" wonderfully. Advantage was taken of Warrington's temporary slackaess and S James scored a try. Just at this stage Hallam had a bad spell and atfer several rrestakes lost the ball on tbeline,another try accruing to Broughton followed by a goal. This aroused excitement to a high pitch, as.only 3 prints separated the teams. Warrington rallied, and Smith and Eden both scored what appeared to be excellent cries in qoick succession. They ware disallowed, but Warrington held the upper hand to the close, the backs defending with the utmost coolness and resource. It is seldom that Warrington do well when Mr. Smith has charge of the whistle, but on this occasion the well- known referee brought luck to Warrington. The try be aaowed Burgess was quite unfair, but I think it wad counter balanced by tries which Isherwood, Smith and Eden all scored with apparent fairness. However, we won, and this is the main thing after all. Moreover the more does not represent Warrington's superiority. Twenty points to five would have been nearer the mark, for the home backs were completely outclassed. --- Bate made a wonderful difference to Warrington and played with something like his old skill, and all his old judgment. Burgess cottoned on to his peculiar ways at once, and the pair were irresistible. The Flixton youth is coming out rapidly. Salford have missed something I Fish, Isherwood,Smith and Jones worked like a machine, the two centres playing the proper game. Snai'.h gave a display very much different to what he has given lately. lam in hep..s that the sceptical Warrington crowd will soon ve him in his best form—against Oldham perhaps. He is a good player, as I have said before, but does not always do himself justice—and oft suer than not it is his own fault. Hallam played a fair game, kicking strongly, but showing a lack of calmness and confidence -wheel cornered. The forwards played with more dash than for some time, Antrobas and Eden being especially pro- minent. The Himmel man is a goad capture. The Rangers appear to - have deteriorated sadly, and beyond a good pack they have a shockingly poor team. We ought to have beaten them at Warrington, but they are much easier prey now. Barran and the two young James's were the only men who played with any skill on Saturday. Jackson's presence would have meant a lot, but fortunately for Warrington the "big un "was kept at BlarkpOol by the military authorities. Tkoy were afraid be might get hurt. Sankey Harriers. Tao above well -known club had Sacred Heart Harriers (St. Helens) at their headquarters, the Sloop Hotel, Sankey, en Saturday, for the second inter-311lb run of the season, also the 7 miles championship final race was set down for decision. The trail was laid over a course of good country of about 8 miles, by way of Rose-lane, Burtonwood, across tha fields to Bold, corning out at Peuketh, and finished a good two miles on the road. The runners (16 of Sankey and 18 of Sacred Heart) were despatched on their journey at 4 o'clock, and the first man to arrive home was J Wilding, of Sankey. The race was rather a tame one, es Sankey had the first thirteen home, winning easily by 63 points. The .visi- tors were cntertainel to tea provided by the home club, and a pleasant evening was spent. The following team has been chosen by the Committee to represent the club in the Northern Cross-Country Junior Championship held on Rotherham Racecourse next Saturday, and in which race they are labelled " dangerous" for junior honours, of either first, second or third :—G Eastwood, T Devlin, Joseph Riley, L Green, R Throasell, J Wilding, JiPotts, J Prince, W Lawton.
